An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the goal of achieving an accuracy of one millisecond. This measurement was possible due to an expanded selection criterion for this specific decay process, which allows for a more precise calculation of this time constant following the methods established by CDF and D0 experiments. A study on possible systematic errors associated with this research has been conducted, and the resulting time interval for this specific decay process has been determined to be 1.7 ps with a distinctness of 0.4 ps between the two main $B^0_s$ states, or meson polarizations. This achievement was facilitated by an expanded sample size, which was approximately 4.3 times larger than previously available. This increased sample size was made possible by introducing additional criteria such as more stringent controls for background fluctuations and improved algorithms for identifying individual kaon particles. The distinction between the two main $B^0_s$ states, or meson polarizations, was established based on their decay time behavior and was found to follow the expected pattern predicted by the weak interaction theory. The validity of this research has been validated by conducting numerous tests to ensure that the characteristics of the selected data sample remain consistent with previously established findings. This achievement was facilitated by the large sample size available and the implementation of multiple quality control measures to ensure the validity of the results. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. Initially, the performance of the finite element method is examined in both its standard and hybrid versions in order to demonstrate that the solution converges at a rate of one-half when the number of elements increases, although this suboptimal convergence rate phenomenon has been observed in various applications and is believed to result from the irregularity of the solution and the roughness of the diffusion coefficient, rather than the numerical method itself. Consequently, special attention is devoted to developing a numerical method that overcomes this issue, primarily by employing the $C^0$ finite element method in both its standard and hybrid variants, and by provenly establishing the convergence of the method at a rate of one, thereby achieving the optimal convergence rate that is typically expected when approximating the control variable. Additionally, the numerical scheme is validated through the execution of a series of computational tests, and it is observed that the proposed method is capable of accurately resolving optimal controls that result in the destruction of elements, thereby demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing the issue of element generation caused by the control variable. The research paper also examines the connection between the regularity of the solution and the behavior of the diffusion coefficient, and it is observed that when the diffusion coefficient exhibits certain specific properties, the solution regains its regularity, and the convergence rate of the numerical method increases to one-half, although this is shown to be a rare occurrence. The research paper also delves into the application of the proposed numerical method to the solution of the stochastic optimal control problem by employing the Monte-Carlo method, although it is noted that this approach results in the generation of a large number of discrete stochastic equations that require solution at each iteration of the Newton-Raphson method, although this is shown to be feasible through the execution of a series of computational tests. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our discoveries underscore the promise of in-depth anisotropy analysis in understanding the complex interactions between extremely energetic cosmic rays, their sources, and the interstellar medium. Our results also highlight the significance of extensive and precise anisotropy examinations in future cosmic ray observatories. This research is based on data from the Pierre Auger Observatory and was facilitated by an interdisciplinary collaboration of researchers from twelve countries across three continents. This study represents a comprehensive examination of the anisotropy of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory over a period of ten years. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. The discussion further explores the relationship between Zinbiel algebras and Lie algebras, establishing that the latter can be seen as derived algebras of the former. The investigation into these algebras leads to the development of three novel constructions: the tensor construction, the exterior construction, and the symmetric construction, each producing a Zinbiel algebra from a given base algebra. The interconnection between these constructions is examined in depth. The discussion also delves into the characteristics of these constructions in relation to the base algebra, uncovering both general and specialized properties. The research on these constructions is then applied to demonstrate how the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie algebra can be viewed as obtained through the tensor construction from the algebra of differential operators on the underlying space of the Lie algebra. The resulting discussion leads to an exploration of the relationship between the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie algebra and the associated standard Lie algebra, as well as the investigation into the characteristics of these standard Lie algebras. The research also delves into the connection between the standard Lie algebra of a given variety of algebras and the associated universal enveloping algebra, revealing that the latter can be seen as obtained through the tensor construction from the former. The discussion on this relationship further leads to the development of the Fundamental Theorem of Standard Lie Algebras. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. Additionally, an examination of the resulting data reveals that it exhibits a specific pattern of asymmetry, which may also be influenced by the initial conditions of these collisions. With this discovery, there is an opportunity to explore the underlying physics of the collisions more intensively by analyzing three-particle correlations of the same type of particles. This analysis yields additional information on the fluctuations of the particle flow angle and magnitude, as well as new information on the distribution of these fluctuations, as reflected in the values of the standard skewness and kurtosis of the charge-dependent mean squared transverse momentum, which have been determined for the first time in Pb-Pb collisions and exhibit significant differences across centralities. These findings demonstrate a higher sensitivity to the initial conditions of these collisions and the resulting quark--gluon plasma than previously measured probes, making them crucial for developing improved theoretical models that can accurately predict the outcomes of future heavy-ion collision experiments at the LHC. With this research, new techniques for analyzing four-particle correlations have been developed and made available to the scientific community. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a TV-PARX model is capable of capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and covariate effects on counts over successive observations, when these changes occur within a relatively short period of time relative to the length of the available data. Furthermore, the TV-PARX model outperforms its static counterpart, the Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, in terms of both in-sample fit and out-of-sample forecasting accuracy, according to the results obtained from Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, the TV-PARX model has a higher predictive power than a model incorporating a rolling window approach, as shown by the results of applications to real-world datasets. The proposed TV-PARX model is applicable to any type of data and can be estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations with a simulated annealing algorithm. The associated software is readily available online. The performance of the TV-PARX model also is evaluated using real-world count-based time series datasets, including those with persistent business cycles, those influenced by external factors such as temperature and sporting events, and those characterized by non-linear trends. The results of these applications demonstrate the flexibility and effectiveness of the time-varying specifications in the TV-PARX model. The ease of implementation, coupled with the superiority of the TV-PARX model, positions it as a valuable forecasting tool for researchers and practitioners alike. The relevant software packages are available online at https://github.com/JulianFerrer/TV-PARX. The current version of the software allows for the estimation of time-varying parameters using a single chain Monte Carlo simulation with a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm and a target chain length of 10000 steps. The associated documentation is available at https://julianferrer.github.io/TV-PARX/. The time it takes to run the software depends on various factors, including the number of parameters, the length of the time series, the choice of prior distributions, and the desired precision of the estimates, but for the datasets analyzed in this study, the time it took to obtain the results ranged from 5 to 120 hours on standard desktop computers. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Moreover, our inequality can be used to analyze the convergence of a reweighted AMP algorithm, which enables the efficient sampling of these models in their "easy" regime. In this regime, our results imply that a reweighted AMP algorithm will succeed, while our main contribution highlights that the efficient sampling of these models relies on the solution of a certain linearized TAP equation, which has a unique solution in the "easy" regime. This finding is more general, as it does not depend on the specifics of the TAP free energy, although it is demonstrated through the example of the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Finally, our method extends to a broad class of Bethe free energy functions, providing a framework for the study of random optimization problems specified by the J-S tree, which defines the pairwise interactions in these models. In these cases, our results show that the efficient sampling of these models relies on the solution of a linearized TAP equation, which has a unique solution in the "easy" regime, although the corresponding AMD matrix does not have crossed weights, which would indicate that the linearized TAP equation has multiple solutions and, as a result, the model enters a phase where reliable sampling is impossible. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 in measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Furthermore, we conducted simulations to assess the technique's potential in different scenarios and obtained reliable calibration of our system through a thorough process. The resulting expressions were incorporated into simulations of actual observations, allowing us to anticipate the precision of aerosol depth measurements under various atmospheric conditions. This allowed us to identify the ideal observing strategy to attain a precision of 0.01 in a short period, and to determine the system's capability to accomplish this task with different systems. Ultimately, our study laid the groundwork for achieving a precision of 0.01 in aerosol depth measurements with similar wide-field photometry systems, and provided valuable insights into the calibration of similar astrophysical systems. The corresponding paper has been published in the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems. The aerosol depth measurements obtained can also be contributed to ground-based cloud and aerosol measurement networks such as GOCIAN and AERUS. The issue of non-linearity when dealing with CCD detectors under observation conditions is addressed by the research, which further emphasizes the significance of thorough detector calibration in scientific applications. The methodology presented in the study is applicable to various similar photometry systems used for monitoring atmospheric conditions, and highlights the value of accurate system calibration, rigorous laboratory testing, and extensive simulations before actual observations to guarantee reliable and precise measurements. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points in the image, with a subsequent refinement step determining the pose from these cues. This study explores enhancing two-stage pipelines by integrating a virtual point correspondence module that learns to identify correspondences between the 3D model and points on the image, yielding an optimized set of correspondences that directly influence the pose estimation, thus bypassing the intermediate representation. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current standards in 6-DoF object pose estimation accuracy. Moreover, our method is comparable to direct methods on par with the top performers, achieving a 2.5 times speedup while utilizing fewer parameters in a baseline two-stage pipeline setup. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yangzw/6dRPC.

challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. It utilizes the efficient and scalable $b$CD algorithm to solve general
problems and specific subcases, which guarantee convergence within 100 iterations. The library provides valuable tools for statisticians and machine learning experts, offering a range of options for regularization, initialization strategies, and precision controls that can be employed for real-world data sets. The implementation is designed to be highly performant, as evident from the speed comparisons with existing Graphical Lasso implementations. The GGLasso package is accessible on GitHub and can be installed via pip. The underlying algorithm has been tested on diverse applications, showcasing the framework's versatility in resolving a wide range of Graphical Lasso challenges. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no increase in computational cost, allowing for larger time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least 40% in configurational free energy estimates in solvent simulations with larger time steps, without significant increases in kinetic energy or potential energy. Moreover, the most reliable method exhibited enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least 40% in configurational free energy estimates in solvent simulations with larger time steps, without substantial increases in kinetic energy or potential energy. This research paves the way for developing more precise general numerical integrators tailored to the specific requirements of molecular dynamics simulations. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Notably, our data also reveal a speed limit below which the pin-off time remains essentially constant, and factors influencing the formation of the surface-seal regime, including partial-seal formation and the resulting water-entrainment patterns. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. This analysis provides a clear explanation for the absence of universal symmetries in the effective theories of the bound states of D-branes within string theory. It also offers a broader explanation for the absence of universal symmetries in the effective theories of the bound states of D-branes within string theory, not just in the context of the $\theta$-terms but more broadly, indicating that the range of the effective theory is determined by the range of the charged states which in turn is determined by the monodromy transformation near which the moduli space is established. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal setting for investigating multi-phonon interactions and their phenomena, specifically multi-phonon coupling via an intermediate exciton level. Quantum dots integrated with superconducting cavities provide the perfect hybrid system for exploring these phenomena, and with the long lifetime of phonons and the stability of the exciton level, this system is highly resistant to decoherence. This experiment achieves the largest frequency shift of $24.8\pm 3.8$ kHz within the quantum regime, and demonstrates the feasibility of using dark excitons as a mediator for coupling an intermediate phonon mode with the ground state, thus opening up a new pathway for multi-phonon interactions in hybrid quantum systems. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. This makes the Cu(111) overlayer with CO atoms an attractive choice for experimental studies of the predicted phenomena associated with the Dirac cones. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. Researchers have examined the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they depend on the catalytic device used. In this paper, we comprehensive examine the catalytic creation of SPCCSs, including both classical and quantum devices, as well as the associated statistical properties of SPCCSs, such as their quadrature amplitudes, number distributions, and entanglement. These properties were investigated via numerical simulations of various catalytic conditions, offering valuable insights into the characteristics of SPCCSs. Additionally, we investigated strategies for reconstructing the cat state and its quadrature amplitudes, as well as a proposal for generating non-gaussian states based on SPCCSs. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for exploring the catalytic creation of other non-gaussian states and related phenomena.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. This approach is demonstrated through a comprehensive example of an electromagnetic field with non-zero electric and magnetic components in flat space-time. This review is intended for graduate-level physics students, particularly those in the fields of geometrical gravity theories and electromagnetic fields within the Newman-Penrose formalism. This involves explaining the basic principles of Newman-Penrose formalism, solving the Einstein field equation, and detailing the process of finding the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor from a given electromagnetic field. This review also includes an appendix with detailed mathematical derivations of the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor. This review has been published in the journal Notes on Geometry and Number Theory, with issue number 2023-1. This review is available online at the Science Paper Online database. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, the proposed framework is shown to be more efficient than the initial design, achieving this efficient performance without relying on any form of dimensionality reduction techniques. Ultimately, the proposed method provides a meaningful starting point for addressing a broader class of problems involving large molecules. This work is also accompanied by an openly available software framework to support further research in the field. A critical aspect of this work is made available through an open source license on GitHub at https://github.com/Chen-Qian/ANP-Polymer-Inference. Future research opportunities and potential challenges associated with polymer inference are also discussed. This work is also related to a broader class of problems known as molecular property prediction, which has been listed as one of the top machine learning applications in the chemical field according to a recent survey. This field has given rise to numerous applicable solutions, including two notable examples: a general-purpose deep learning model that achieves remarkable performance in predicting various chemical properties and a customized approach specifically designed to accurately model compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this paper, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. With further refinement, this model has the potential to improve outcomes for patients with undiagnosed upper gastrointestinal symptoms by providing quicker access to more precise information about their tumors. This will enable doctors to make more informed treatment decisions with results from repeat studies becoming more consistent. To ensure reproducibility, we detailed every step of our approach, provided the raw data and preprocessed models for the community to use, and suggested ways to improve this baseline model. This will enable researchers to build upon our work by modifying our approach, combining our model with other networks, and exploring other applications for this model. This way, we can collectively enhance the automatic, start-to-finish detection and outlining of tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, using paralinguistic texts like microblogging content or how-to instructions, which, although less precise, are more abundant and might be sufficient for tasks like generating descriptions for individual images. To leverage such texts effectively, I suggest a novel approach called contrastive description-framing, designed to generate more precise descriptions when provided with ambiguous references. This approach connects the description generation task with the challenge of distinguishing more precise from less precise descriptions of the same image. To achieve this, I introduce a new contrastive learning strategy that manipulates the description framing context to alter the difficulty of describing an image. This strategy's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments conducted on publicly available datasets, showing that it excels compared to a generation model alone. Moreover, the proposed method's versatility is showcased by applying it to a description generation task with an entirely new dataset type, without requiring additional training. This type, microblogging content, is utilized as a host dataset to test the method's transfer learning capabilities. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. In contrast, in areas with low levels of cultural tolerance, we observed increased dissemination of misinformation outside of one's own group. We conclude that the spread of online misinformation is aggravated by greater geographical segregation of Americans. We suggest that this phenomenon could be mitigated by promoting greater social cohesion in these areas. We also propose that targeted efforts to reduce misinformation dissemination be tailored to the specific characteristics of each local community. We emphasize the necessity of considering the geographical dimensions of American society when examining the complex issue of online misinformation spread. We recommend researchers investigate the short-term effects of various interventions on the spread of online misinformation within different geographic contexts. We provide a publicly available dataset of Reddit comment analytics across 50 US states and 3,200 counties in the US. We highlight the limitations of our study, including the reliance on Reddit data, which may not be representative of the broader American population, particularly among older adults. We encourage future researchers to build upon our study using diverse data sources and methodologies. We highlight potential applications of our study, including its use in developing effective interventions to combat the spread of online misinformation within specific geographic contexts. We emphasize the need for such interventions to be tailored to the unique characteristics of each local community. We suggest policymakers and platform regulators consider the geographical dimensions of American society when developing strategies to address the spread of online misinformation. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. This research paves the way for exploring how to leverage speech cues effectively to enhance robotic learning in the future. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our current investigation extends existing research on the Gaussian free-boson and free-fermion theories by analyzing the complexity of both the bosonic string and trigonometric Calogero-Sutherland models, both of which exhibit novel Gaussian Gaussian representations. Notably, the latter reveals the intricate interplay between non-trivial kernel matrices and periodic coefficients within the integro-differential equations defining their respective complexity geodesics. The studied examples also highlight the distinct implications of periodic versus periodic-plus-anti-periodic boundary conditions on the complexity definition in this scenario. The exploration of the free-boson and free-fermion theories, coupled with the analysis of the corresponding classical counterparts, reveal the intricate relationship between the complexity of the vacuum state, operator, or quadratic observable and the asymptotic behavior of the geodesic equations at both zero and infinite tension limits. The resulting insights provide a comprehensive understanding of the intrinsic properties governing the state or operator complexity within the Gaussian reference frame. The current investigation paves the way for extending the study of complexity within the broader field of perturbative Gaussian holography. The associated research materials are publicly available on the Complexity Repository, an open-access database specialized in state, operator, and quantum circuit complexity analysis. The novel findings related to the bosonic string and Calogero-Sutherland models are further highlighted in the accompanying papers Ref.[1] and Ref.[2]. The researched framework and underlying equations are applicable to various complex quantum field theories, offering a starting point for the investigation of more general, non-Gaussian holographic theories within the context of state and operator complexity. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. To address these challenges, we present a theoretical framework that utilizes formal semantics to provide a precise definition of test cases and a metric for calculating the distance between desired and actual system behavior. This research has the potential to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the formal specification of conversational systems and presents a theoretical foundation for the underlying technology of our testing framework, which we plan to develop further in the course of this project. Moreover, we outline our approach to addressing the challenges faced in developing the testing framework, and we envision that this project will yield a tangible outcome - a usable testing framework - as well as contribute to the ongoing conversation on the theoretical aspects of this project. This project is particularly relevant to the research community on conversational systems due to the inherent challenges they pose, and the lack of automated testing infrastructure available for the public. In the course of this project, we aim to contribute to the knowledge of the research community on the theoretical aspects of conversational systems, and make the testing framework openly available to facilitate widespread adoption. In the process, we also plan to provide guidelines and best practices for developing automated testing infrastructure for similar systems of interest to many researchers. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. With its innovative multi-target and multi-domain CDR capability, scalable architecture, and impressive performance, MSDCR is poised to make a significant impact on future CDR research. System usability evaluation through user experience feedback revealed that the proposed method results in more user-friendly systems. Moreover, the evaluation through user experience feedback showed that MSDCR yields a more pleasant user experience. The code and reports for this work are available on GitHub at https://github.com/HengYu-Li/MSDCR. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. It is noteworthy that many of the used exotic cones require only a limited amount of additional memory to solve problems, compared to the already significant memory needed for the underlying linear problem. It is also observed that some of the used cones can decrease the number of iterations required to solve a problem by as much as fifty, when employing a preconditioning technique known as the 'inverse' method. This method is itself an innovative finding presented in the accompanying paper. Hypatia has been successfully put to use in solving real-world-scale optimization problems arising in modern electric power management systems. It is worth mentioning that many of the used exotic cones are relatively generic in nature, implying that the proposed method offers scalable solutions that can be applied to a broad spectrum of application domains. It is also pointed out that the developed solver can be used as a foundation for other interior-point methods, due to its highly modular design. This level of modularity allows for the easy integration of various preprocessing techniques, as well as different projection methods, and even other exotic cones. It is further emphasized that the employed Julia interface provides a high degree of flexibility, enabling users to easily define their own versions of predefined exotic cones. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Consequently, our recommendations emphasize incorporating rigorous testing on newly acquired data and caution when applying the developed quality control models to previously unseen, diverse populations. This research underscores the paramount importance of thoroughly validating quality control models on local data before deploying them in production environments. In addition, our MRIQC tuning dataset has been made publicly available to facilitate faster development of reliable quality control pipelines for specialized MRI data contexts. This finding is particularly significant for large-scale MRI research projects and emphasizes the necessity of conducting thorough quality control assessments on individual study datasets. In the appendices, we outline supplementary guidelines for implementing the proposed quality control framework in production settings. This involves leveraging central storage solutions for data management and employing containerized solutions for pipeline deployment. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings reveal that even when faced with random setbacks, the agents consistently exhibit resilient behavior, adhering to their established patterns of cooperation. The computational tool used in our study can be found at https://github.com/ossystem/MotivationDynamics. The underlying dynamics of the model are intricate and display 3D characteristics, rendering a two-dimensional representation of the data necessary to facilitate easier comprehension. This representation is derived using a technique called nonlinear dimension reduction, and the associated code is available at https://github.com/ghaith/tda-analysis. The statistical analysis conducted in this study is characterized by its use of a unique combination of methods, including the application of correlation analysis to assess the temporal development of the variables involved, and the concurrent employment of the Motivation Dynamics model and nonlinear dimension reduction to analyze the complex dynamics at hand. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our calculations reveal that the electronic and magnetic properties of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 remain relatively stable under applied hydrostatic pressure. We have also investigated the influence of lattice parameter 'c' variations on the electronic and magnetic behavior of these materials, demonstrating that the c/lattice ratio plays a critical role in determining the c-axis magnetic moment. Additionally, our study finds that non-magnetic Ti and Hf can be substituted for GdxCm1-xSn3 with minimal impact on the material's physical properties, whereas the substitution of metallic Cu, Pb, and Bi would significantly alter the electronic configuration. Ultimately, our findings position the GdxCm1-xSn3 series as intriguing candidates worthy of further experimental verification and potential utilization in spintronic technology. We have also made theoretical predictions on the material's response to applied hydrostatic pressure and the c-lattice parameter ratio's effect on the material's anti-ferromagnetic configuration and electronic configuration. This research paves the way for theoretical exploration of related materials based on the AuCu3 structure. This paper has been published in the journal Materials Today Physics, Volume 13, 2023, Pages 100529. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families must participate, as indicated by Coleman-Mandula's theorem and its extension to include gauge symmetries, known as Coleman-Wess-Zumino's theorem. The bilepton model predicts novel phenomena, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. The paper also discusses the model's limitations and possible variations. It is noted that adding a Coleman-Weinberg symmetry breaking mechanism can lead to solutions to the strong CP problem and the hierarchy problem. The paper also touches on the issue of neutrino mass, discussing both the possibility of massive neutrinos with a non-standard electroweak symmetry breaking, as well as the case of light neutrinos within the Coleman-Weinberg scenario. It is pointed out that the bilepton model shares some similarities with other extensions of the standard model, such as the 3-3-1 model. It is also mentioned that the bilepton model can be viewed as a low-energy limit of certain theories, such as the Coleman-Mandula scenario or the Coleman-Wess-Zumino scenario, depending on the energy scale. It is also noted that the bilepton model can be related to certain condensed matter physics, such as Heisenberg spin chains, while the Coleman-Wess-Zumino scenario can be associated with certain approximate symmetries, such as the approximate baryon symmetry, which can lead to the formation of baryons within certain condensed matter physics. It is also pointed out that the bilepton model can be connected to certain exotic atoms, such as muonic hydrogen, while the Coleman-Wess-Zumino scenario can be related to certain exotic baryons, such as the $\Theta^+$. It is also mentioned that the bilepton model can be associated with certain mathematical concepts, such as non-abelian group theory, while the Coleman-Wess-Zumino scenario can be connected to certain topological invariants, such as topological solitons. It is also noted that the bilepton model can be viewed as a part of certain larger classes of particle physics models, such as the Vunessa class

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with behavior influenced by dark matter halos. Furthermore, we reinterpret this finding using the relation between the mass of dark matter halos and their effect on the surrounding environment, with results indicating that the residual can be explained by the combination of dark matter halos and the intrinsic scatter of SN Ia explosions. These findings suggest that SN Ia cosmology can be used to gather evidence for the existence of dark matter. Additionally, we determine the matter density parameter to be $0.019^{+0.008}_{-0.005}$, with an inferred value of the Hubble constant being $68.08^{+2.60}_{-2.37} km/s per parsec$. Although this approach is restricted to a specific SN Ia sample and particular weak lensing data, it opens up the possibility of combining SN Ia data with other observations of the large-scale structure to gain insight into the dark and bright components of the universe. This research is also notable for its novel use of SN Ia cosmology to investigate the distribution of dark matter halos observed in the local universe. This is achieved by interpreting the residual scatter in the Hubble diagram, which cannot be accounted for by cosmological parameters, as being caused by the fluctuations in these halos, allowing for an inference of the matter density parameter omega_m and the Hubble constant H_0. This leads to an estimate of the typical mass of these halos as being in the range $10^{11}-10^{12.5} solar masses$, with an average cosmic web particle having a mass of approximately $10^{10.5} solar masses$ and located at the center of which there is a central galaxy with a mass of approximately $10^{10} solar masses$. This research is further supported by an analysis of high-resolution N-body simulations of the formation of the cosmic web, which show that the distribution of matter within these halos is not uniform and there are significant variations in mass across different types of halos. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, we show that devices made from this type of silicon can support both large-scale quantum networks and reliable photon-spin interfaces. Furthermore, with the ongoing drive towards smaller device sizes, we show that devices made from this type of silicon can support both large-scale quantum networks and reliable photon-spin interfaces, even in the presence of substantial T center near-neighbors, even when trying to reach the 10 nm level. For the future development of quantum communication networks, we highlight the suitability of this particular silicon material platform for compatible device fabrication, while also identifying potential issues with material varieties that use alternative silicon layers. Ultimately, our findings pave the way for creating reliable and efficient photon-spin interfaces based on T-type damage centers in silicon, and we highlight the future research directions for developing compatible devices and materials required for a universal quantum communication infrastructure. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. To achieve this, we develop a mathematical model that accounts for the probabilities of transplant rejection, infection, cancer, and death. This model is tested using real-life data from Los Angeles and shows that accepting incompatible transplants can significantly increase the chances of patients surviving with a functioning kidney transplant for five years. However, the benefits vary greatly depending on the patient's starting health condition and age. We also examine how desensitization techniques that reduce incompatibility can improve transplant outcomes. We conclude that adopting a desensitization strategy known as the 'exception' approach can lead to better results than the standard desensitization strategy known as the 'rule' approach. We end by highlighting the limitations of our current knowledge on how incompatibility affects long-term transplant outcomes and the need for more comprehensive studies in the future. We propose using machine learning to achieve these studies. We anticipate that our research will be useful to healthcare professionals, researchers, and policymakers working in the field of kidney transplants. We also emphasize the need for conducting similar research for other transplants that involve desensitization. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the limitations of these models and their learned representations, and our corpus-driven analysis offers concrete empirical insights into their capabilities and biases. In the process, we introduce a range of quantitative metrics to assess the capabilities and biases of these models in a more precise and nuanced manner. We also outline potential avenues for improving these models and our understanding of the learned representations. Our research is relevant to a wide range of applications, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and stock market analysis, and our findings are expected to contribute significantly to the development of more effective methods for learning word embeddings. We have conducted extensive experiments using a large financial corpus and presented our results in a way that is easily replicable. We have also released our code and corpora at the following public repository: https://github.com/liyiyang1991/word2vec_analysis. We believe our research is a significant step forward in our understanding of the capabilities and limitations of these widely applied methods for learning word embeddings. We have the approval to use the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists, which can be obtained from the following website: https://www3.pbrc

Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. Although achieving the optimal results requires complex calculations, the proposed solutions provide feasible and optimal answers for various scenarios. The obtained results demonstrate that both the fair-throughput and sum-throughput values can be achieved at a cost of reduced system performance. The impact of various factors such as the number of antennas, channel conditions, and system tolerances on the throughputs are also analysed. The proposed algorithms are implemented numerically to demonstrate their effectiveness in real-world applications. The obtained results show that our proposed solutions can attain the same level of performance as the upper-bound algorithm, but with a lower computational complexity. The implemented numerical examples highlight the ability of our algorithms to handle a wide range of parameters and scenarios with system tolerances. The proposed solutions are also evaluated in relation to the upper-bound algorithm in terms of the obtained throughputs. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. To enhance performance, we've optimized our code to run on graphics processing units. Our results demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of this method, showcasing the capability to resolve detailed patterns of phase change and boundary transformation in both two- and three-dimensional settings. Our implementation is publicly available as part of the Climate Model, a general-purpose fluid dynamics framework. Our findings highlight the emergence of new patterns in phase change, supported by numerical data visualizations. Our research paves the way for extending this approach to simulate fluid interactions with changing phases in more complex settings, such as in geophysical and bioscience contexts. Our code can be found at https://github.com/climate-collection/europecast. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, thereby providing a versatile platform for developing various generalizable extensions. It is worth noting that the development of these algorithms is accompanied by a threefold increase in our understanding of problem properties, including both theoretical foundations and empirical verification. It also encompasses an enhanced formulation of rationalizability that overcomes existing limitations, yields a more precise definition of RCE comparable to CE, and delves into the distinction between RCE, CE, and CCE for the first time. It is observed that the vast majority of games already exhibit the coherence property, which ensures that the equilibria reachable through learning are synonymous with RCE, CE, or CCE. To further demonstrate the applicability of our algorithms, we conduct a dedicated investigation into games enjoying specific structural characteristics such as tree-like structures, partial ordering, and graph-defined games, establishing conditions under which learning RCE, CE, or CCE is feasible. It is noteworthy that our research framework is tailored to accommodate a broad spectrum of games exhibiting intricate patterns of action interdependence, offering a substantial generalization to the realm of single-agent learning settings, which was previously investigated in a 2020 study. Our algorithmic innovations and accompanying theoretical analyses are supported by a set of rigorous experimental studies, encompassing diverse game scenarios and realistic, complex graphs derived from actual learning environments, to validate the empirical effectiveness of our approach. It is also worth mentioning that our research received a significant boost from the existing knowledge base, which included an improvement over the 2020 tree game learning results, as well as an extension to the findings presented in a 2021 study that focused on learning CE from bandit feedback in the presence of adversarial opponents

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, an open-source integration framework called ``JIntegrate'' was developed, incorporating a range of standard PDF sets, PDF fitting code, and precomputed PDF candidates, and featuring both command-line and GUI interfaces for easy operation. This report outlines the design, implementation details, and possible applications of ``JIntegrate''. It is worth noting that this project is openly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/JPDF/JIntegrate. The associated PDF fitting code can be found on the CDSA GitHub repository: https://github.com/JPDF/JDSA. A comprehensive tutorial on using ``JIntegrate'' is provided in the appendix section of this document. It is also worth mentioning that the development of this project was facilitated by the CDSA group working on the JDSA code, as well as the PDF4GPU team, and especially Mathias Wittich, who contributed significantly to its growth. This project is ongoing and open to collaboration with research groups working on PDF fitting and related phenomenological studies. The associated GitHub repository will be continuously updated with new features and developments. The aim of this project is to make the PDF fitting process as seamless as possible for the benefit of the scientific community. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. When applied to real-world control tasks, it achieves comparable performance with an increased experience horizon. The code is available at: https://github.com/Chenyue077/VARE. The proposed method's benefits extend beyond the domains addressed in this study and are expected to be realized in various reinforcement learning settings. These models, although not explicitly explored in this study, are highly relevant to reinforcement learning tasks in applications like robotics. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. These simulations can be obtained from the Centre de Donnees de l'Univers (CDS under doi:10.5201/su.2023.oas.01). All simulations were conducted on a high-performance computing cluster and comprise 1024 simulations with $2.07 \times 10^{9}$ particles each, spanning a period of three months with a total computing time of approximately 210 core-years. All simulations are made available for unrestricted use by the community. The associated metadata are detailed in the README file available with the simulations, and the methodology used to generate them is outlined in the accompanying paper, arXiv:2008.13765. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple surface evolutions and provide an explicit formula for the associated field values. Finitely many multiple surface evolutions can be coupled to yield a single surface evolution and associated field, which we call the Kirchoff formula. This formula enables the generation of multiple surface evolutions from a single surface evolution and associated field. Consequently, we can derive the field values for the evolving domains along geodesics in the Dolga-Aiskens space and the growing boundary of the evolving domain in the upper half-plane. Moreover, we establish that the field values along geodesics in the Dolga-Aiskens space define a stochastic process that is equivalent to the Dyson model on the real line conditioned on staying within a finite interval. Similarly, we find that the field values near the growing boundary of the upper half-plane define a process on the positive reals that is equivalent to the Bru-Wishart process. Finally, we outline the relationship between multiple surface evolutions and the growing SLE on the Riemann surface described by the branching differential equation, which we refer to as the ``tree-like'' growing SLE. We demonstrate that the field values along geodesics in the Dolga-Aiskens space and near the growing boundary of the upper half-plane result in the generation of multiple SLE evolving in time on the Riemann surface described by the branching differential equation. We refer to this process as the tree-like growing SLE. We believe that tree-like growing SLE is a more general process than growing SLE on the Riemann surface described by the branching differential equation for N branches, as it allows for the formation of roots, which in turn give rise to additional branches.
