MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. 
The extension's extensive range of advanced capabilities is matched only by the
degree of difficulty users face when attempting to install and configure it. 
Despite WorkingWiki's remarkable capabilities, its relatively small user base
suggests there are barriers to adoption that require addressing, as evidenced
by the presence of unused features and the limited scale of its most notable
implementation. Nevertheless, the core ideology underlying WorkingWiki remains
sound, and it has inspired the creation of related projects and spin-offs. 
To build upon WorkingWiki's foundation, the extension has been reworked to work
with the latest version of MediaWiki, and the resulting 'WorkingWiki 2.0' is
an improved, more modular version that is easier to use and customize. 
As the name 'WorkingWiki 2.0' suggests, this revised extension represents a
significant improvement over its precursor, and it boasts a range of new features
that address the shortcomings of the original version. These improvements are
intended to make WorkingWiki more user-friendly, more adaptable to diverse uses,
and more maintainable in the face of future development.

transforming it from a monolithic extension into a collection of distinct, reusable
components that can be combined in innovative ways. This revised architecture
enables users to customize WorkingWiki by selecting the features they need for
their projects, and it facilitates the creation of derived extensions that can
be used for entirely different purposes.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. The perfect fluid scenario is also examined as well as the case of rotating test particles within a nonlocal gravitational field. The resulting geodesic equations lead to the same expression for the perihelion precession as general relativity. The connection to the nonlocal gravity theory's original variables is established using a new approach that was initially proposed by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The implications of not accounting for the nonlocal nature of the gravitational field when investigating extremely dense objects or high-energy phenomena are discussed. The relationship between nonlocal gravity theory and f(R)-gravity is also examined. The paper's conclusions include the nonlocal equivalent of $f(R)$-gravity and the prediction that the value of R will approach zero in the nonlocal context. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capacity for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In both cases, we tracked how the objects evolved over time, transforming from hydrogen-burning stars into brown dwarfs. This led to the creation of theoretical phase diagrams that account for rotation in addition to other key factors, providing a foundation for understanding the long-term development of low-mass, rapidly rotating stars. This research reveals that rotating low-mass stars have specific mass ranges based on spin, and these ranges can influence how they transition from hydrogen-burning stages to becoming brown dwarfs. This is particularly evident in scenarios where objects lose mass and spin out of control, resulting in different mass ranges for the resulting brown dwarfs, with one range being the so-called "ELOIS" objects, with masses approximately between 0.01 and 0.06 solar masses, and another range that includes super-Jupiter planets with masses approximately between 4 to 7.5 solar masses, and another range that includes objects with masses approximately between 0.055 and 0.1 solar masses, known as "ORCs" (overmassive, radii-reduced objects). This research also suggests that spinning low-mass stars might produce specific types of brown dwarfs, including "ELOIS" objects, and could provide an explanation for the existence of certain giant planets. This study demonstrates that external forces, such as interactions with binary or tertiary companions, that cause stars to spin out of control and shed mass and spin down slowly, can result in different mass ranges for the resulting brown dwarfs, and may explain the diversity observed within the "ELOIS" population and other similar populations of brown dwarfs. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. In the process of achieving this goal, an algorithm has been created that generates all possible representations with the highest number of edge crossings meeting a given threshold, in addition to computing the minimum number of node splits needed for an edge-free representation. The approach has been tested on real-world datasets and demonstrated its capabilities in uncovering all planar variants of a particular graph, as well as the corresponding tangle diagrams, at different levels of complexity. The approach has been implemented within a tool that can be utilized interactively through a graphical interface. The underlying algorithm leverages certain efficient data structures to operate effectively, even with large-scale input data. The developed approach has implications for exploring all ways to represent a bipartite graph without edge crossings, beyond the traditional single representation sought in the majority of research studies. The example use case presented involves the reconstruction of a complex molecular compound from a set of experimental measurements, for which the corresponding reaction graph needs to be represented in a planar manner to facilitate successful prediction via machine learning techniques. The actual implementation is capable of processing graphs comprising up to 50 nodes, and the developed algorithm has been put to use on a range of random graph samples, as well as actual biological and chemical graphs of varying sizes. predictive models. By integrating our robot into simulated environments, we
created a functioning predictive model. This model was trained to predict the
effect of thruster firing on future positions and velocities, allowing it to
select the most beneficial walking pattern. To enhance performance, we introduced
a feedback loop that adjusted the model's predictions to match actual data from
tests, thereby refining its accuracy. As a result, this predictive model excelled
in navigating through complex terrain by choosing the most advantageous steps.

future events on its decision-making, thereby effectively managing risks and
avoiding potentially hazardous situations. Ultimately, our research demonstrated
an significant improvement in applying machine learning to bipedal robots, with
performance gains reflected in lower peak hip angles, greater distance traversed,
and a significant decrease in thruster fires. These advancements were achieved
without any gain scheduling or differential flattening. This approach can be
extended to a broader range of predictive control methods for robotic systems.

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  A discussion on the trade-offs between HyperDegrade, Flush+Reload attacks, and other performance degradation strategies for SMT architectures was also presented, along with recommendations for future work.  The implementation details of HyperDegrade, which was tested on an Intel Core i7 processor, are made available to the community, offering researchers a starting point for side-channel attack development on SMT architectures.  From the findings of this research, it is clear that side-channel attacks on modern architectures are feasible and can be made more effective using HyperDegrade.  Consequently, this research urges the hardware industry to prioritize the development of secure SMT architectures and encourages developers to adopt more comprehensive security policies when employing SMT architectures.  The implementation of HyperDegrade has been made public to facilitate further research in this area. Moreover, the source code associated with this research can be accessed from the following link: https://github.com/alexandresoso/hyperdegrade. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Notably, our findings extend the scope of Zassenhaus's existing results on centralizers within wreath products. Moreover, our research provides an in-depth examination of the relationship between projective and injective modules in relation to wreath products, thereby expanding on the module-related insights derived from our analysis of centralizers. Some of our results also apply to more general variations of wreath products, which we refer to as monoidal products. These results can be found in the final section of our paper. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but this existing work typically focuses on random network disruptions. In contrast, this paper explores the vulnerabilities of non-random networks by examining how attacks that follow critical paths can lead to the collapse of highly influential nodes in networks that have been optimized for efficiency and effectiveness. To achieve this, the study employs numerical examples to investigate how attacks along critical paths affects networks of varying sizes, particularly those that are optimized for high clustering coefficients and node degree. Furthermore, this study provides a theoretical analysis of the relationships between network attacks and the characteristics of networks of varying sizes. Additionally, this research develops an analytical model to assess the vulnerabilities of non-random networks by focusing on the removal of the most influential nodes in networks that have been optimized for high clustering coefficients and node degree. This model demonstrates how networks with varying sizes and characteristics exhibit similar patterns of vulnerability when attacked along critical paths, thereby providing a foundation for further research on network resilience assessment. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. We also discuss potential variations of this design, including one with a suspended endmass configuration, to help inform the ongoing research and potential applications for future detectors. This design can be utilized for existing detectors, providing strategies for upgrading recycling systems, as well as serving as a foundation for the design of future gravitational wave detectors, such as third-generation detectors like Cosmic Explorer or Enhanced DeciHz Observable. This research highlights the sloshing Sagnac interferometer's ability to surpass the quantum limit in the high-frequency range, making it an attractive option for the development of future low-frequency gravitational wave detectors. This work is also relevant to the development of high-end laser interferometric detectors for other fields, such as tabletop gravitational physics and extremely sensitive length measurements. Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces data transfer delays, and significantly boosts overall connectivity. Further analysis reveals that at very high scale levels, the performance improvement becomes even more pronounced due to more distinct reception areas of nearby devices. Moreover, due to reduced reach areas of some devices for large-scale MIMO arrays, a significant performance gap can be observed between devices that do and do not have direct access to the array. To overcome this limitation, a non-overlapping scheduling mechanism for these devices has been proposed along with the new protocol, leading to even greater performance gains in certain scenarios. Finally, this research demonstrates the superior performance of scale-large MIMO arrays in scenarios with many devices, gathering data and operating as a sensor network. To maximize performance in these scenarios, a sensor network algorithm has been developed that ensures that devices with direct access to the array focus primarily on data collection tasks while devices without direct access concentrate on providing connectivity to the array as access points. According to the results obtained, performance gains of more scale-large MIMO arrays are not matched by corresponding increases in backhaul connectivity, leading to data transfer delays. To address this challenge, a non-overlapping scheduling mechanism for these devices has been proposed along with the new protocol, leading to even greater performance gains in certain scenarios. To further validate the performance of scale-large MIMO arrays in scenarios with many devices, gathering data and operating as a sensor network, an extensive simulation environment has been established, reflecting real-world conditions with varying reception areas of nearby devices, varying data collection tasks with different requirements, varying sensor network topologies with many devices, real-time data transfer schedules with non-overlapping access, and varying cascade connectivity configurations with many devices. Furthermore, various research challenges associated with large-scale MIMO arrays in scenarios with many devices are addressed by this research, opening up new research opportunities in areas such as cross-layer design

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain irregularities in these disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as necessary precursors that lead to the creation of small solid particles, and ultimately, planetesimals. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations that model the gas and solid particle interactions in protoplanetary disks. It highlights the distribution of small solid particles, formed through the vertical shear instability, and suggests that their characteristics align with features observed in recent sub-mm/mm wavelength observations. It also predicts findings that future observations with higher sensitivity and resolution will uncover with the aid of advanced telescopes like ALMA and a Next Generation Very Large Array. It is demonstrated that particular features in substructures require the presence of certain magnetic field strengths, putting them within the reach of upcoming observations that will allow for the direct inference of the strength of magnetic fields in these systems. It is also shown that certain substructures appear only in the presence of a non-uniform distribution of solid particles, prompting the need for direct imaging of solid particles in these systems to confirm previous detection claims, and to explore their dynamics and evolution from formation to consolidation into planetesimals. It is forecast that future Gold Standard observations will reveal not only the distribution of substructures but also the conditions necessary for their formation, along with information about the strength of the magnetic field and the state of the solid particles within these systems. It is proposed that future direct imaging of these systems be conducted with the aid of coronagraphs that facilitate the detection of the faint solid particles in the center of these systems, and the study of their dynamics from formation to consolidation into planetesimals. It is also suggested that there are certain substructures that can only be explained with the aid of simulations that model the gas and solid particle interactions in these systems, and that the direct observation of such interactions is necessary to confirm the findings of the current work. It is concluded that the interacting gas and solid particles in these systems give rise to various shapes and forms, and that future observations with the aid of advanced telescopes will directly observe the dynamics and evolution of these interactions in the surrounding disks of young stars. It is finally proposed that future research involves simulating the conditions of Gold Standard observations to confirm the findings

A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Additionally, BigApple predicts a lower upper limit for the tidal quadrupole love number, $k_2$, than several existing relativistic models, and it also lies within the estimated range derived from GW170817. This suggests that BigApple is a plausible explanation for GW190814's secondary component being a neutron star with a mass of 2.60 solar masses. If confirmed, this discovery would expand the known range of neutron star masses. This study demonstrates that a wide range of force combinations can result in similar outcomes, implying that the BigApple parameter set is essentially one of the many possible solutions using different force inputs, but it stands out due to its unique characteristics. If further research verifies the uniqueness of BigApple, it would imply that the set's properties are extremely robust and unlikely to change with varying force inputs. This could be an indication that the BigApple parameter set is close to the actual force that governs neutron star physics. This study explores the possibility of BigApple being related to the density-dependent contact interaction, which is a key component of Nuclear Field Theory. By applying BigApple to finite nuclei and nuclear matter, its predictions demonstrate a high level of consistency with fundamental principles of physics and the behavior of neutron star masses within the GW190814 event's observed range. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. We found that this type of gate is particularly effective at frequency robustness for intermediate chain lengths, and the appropriate laser frequency can be adjusted to prioritize frequency robustness over motion-induced errors, resulting in improved precision over standard Gaussian gates. Additionally, this scheme yields shorter gate durations compared to veritable π-gates based on Rabi rotations, and the required laser power is relatively modest. Moreover, we demonstrate the execution of a three-qubit quantum algorithm following the Hull-Hall-Dresselhaus structure, utilizing approximately 5000 photons per second and achieving an average error of approximately 0.03 compared to the classical reference after the application of a quantum error correction code known as surface code. In the case of four-qubit DRAG beamsplitters, our simulation shows that this type of gate also exhibits robustness against the phase error induced by the laser, and a combination of the DRAG effect and Gaussian modulation can lead to a significant decrease in residual phase error, remaining under one percent for a wide range of laser frequencies and for chains consisting of two to ten ions. We believe that this type of gate is particularly suited for quantum computations executed on medium-scale trapped ion systems. Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Thus, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ emerges as an extraordinary example where Dirac electrons converge with strong interactions and frustration, offering an unprecedented opportunity to explore rare, correlated Dirac physics. Tomorrow's breakthroughs in physics might stem from the singular chemistry and physics governing this one-of-a-kind material.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with improved acceptance and better background estimation, they aim to extend the existing limit by an order of magnitude, covering areas that current production and decay searches have not thoroughly explored. This study also highlights the significance of the "wrong sign" $\pi^0 e^+$ channel in the $K^+ \to \pi^0 \nu \bar\nu$ measurement, which could potentially reach the standard model background of $4.10\times 10^{12}$ events per year with $10^{18}$ pot, or about 0.01 improvements over the current limit with optimal selection cuts. This would allow for a more stringent limit on the effective lepton mixing angle |U_e|^2 for a wide range of effective N lifetimes, extending beyond the beam dump limit for a large portion of the parameter space. This search is expected to be among the most sensitive experiments exploring the effective lepton interaction with masses up to 350 MeV until the end of the 2020s. This will be primarily achieved through the study of the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ and $K^+ \to e^+ e^+ e^-$ processes with optimized detection techniques for the $\pi^0$ and the two photon final states, which will entail installing a lead-scintillator electromagnetic calorimeter in the NA62 experiment's beam acceptance. This new detector will allow for the rejection of background processes due to the distinctive characteristics of the calorimeter, primarily the absence of hadronic neutral showers in the acceptance, in addition to the established particle identification and trigger systems. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Our code has been made publicly accessible on https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

In an inflationary model, with a specific type of $\alpha$-attractor potential, we examine the behavior in the high-$k$ regime, where cosmological perturbations exhibit excessive growth and negative values of the Bardeen potential. This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. We determined the scalar density fluctuations ($\sigma$), asymmetry ($\beta$), and PBH mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{PBH}$) in relation to specific mass scales. Our results reveal the formation of PBHs over the $k$ range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, with corresponding mass ranges and properties. These predictions align with forecasts from LISA and other gravitational wave detectors, with a significant overlap in the $f_\mathrm{PBH}$ estimates. However, the agreement holds only when the relevant $k$-range is limited to a narrow interval, indicating the potential for distinct PBH populations formed in different regions of the sky. Our analysis also yields predictions for the characteristics of PBHs in the $M$-$f_\mathrm{PBH}$ plane, which could be validated through future multi-band GW observations combining LISA, Pulsar Timing Arrays, third-generation GW detectors, and ground-based interferometric detectors like GEO600 and the Giant Metrology for Gravitational Wave Astronomy (GMGA). The estimated formation period corresponds to specific sky regions and evolutionary stages of the universe, with implications for the properties of newly formed PBHs and their eventual merger products. The conditions we found favorable to PBH formation are maintained during a post-inflationary stage known as the "soft exit" phase, during which the universe transitions from an inflationary to a quasi-linear state. This phase is characterized by distinct oscillatory modes of the inflaton field, with potentially distinct PBH formation patterns, albeit with a $k$-range that appears less likely to be detectable through GW observations. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. They also computed the variance of the number of deepest nodes, demonstrating that it scales with the number of nodes and can be determined for large populations, in opposition to standard ordered trees whose variance is undetermined. Additionally, they established an explicit formula for the generating function of the number of deepest nodes, which facilitates further statistical inquires. Given the connection to skew Dyck paths, their findings can be interpreted in terms of area- or height-related properties of these paths. It is worth noting that their findings for marked ordered trees were obtained through distinct probabilistic constructions and path interpretations, yet shared similarities with existing results on standard ordered trees constructed from random rooted planes or oriented maps. Their analysis also uncovered an intriguing relationship with binary search trees constructed from random rooted planes or oriented maps, which were first analyzed by Currie and Lad, providing additional insights into the properties of these trees. In the process, they resolved an open problem from Currie and Lad, regarding the variance of the number of deepest nodes in binary search trees with n nodes. It is important to note that their results for binary search trees were obtained through the connection to marked ordered trees, as the original variables used by Currie and Lad did not lend themselves to this variance calculation. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the limited understanding of risk aversion among storage units, we propose developing risk management frameworks that account for their individual risk profiles. This is crucial for ensuring these systems behave in ways that contribute to the reliability of the grid. We also suggest that storage units be permitted to hedge their energy sales forward in specialized markets, which would allow them to manage their risk more effectively. This could be particularly valuable during peak demand periods or when there are significant imbalances in renewable energy generation. Ultimately, our research underlines the significance of considering the risk-averse characteristics of energy storage systems in order to ensure they operate in a way that maintains the integrity of the grid. This will become increasingly vital as these systems play a larger role in the structure of future power markets. We have made our code and data available online for the sake of reproducibility and further study. This work is a preliminary step towards investigating more complex issues, such as the impact of storage units' risk aversion on market outcomes, and ways to design market mechanisms that account for their individual risk preferences. This will be crucial for developing regulatory frameworks that effectively manage risk in power markets incorporating storage units. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows for the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of selecting more evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Consequently, BASE outperforms random sampling consistently. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. 

Our research demonstrates that combined self-supervised pretraining and active learning fails to yield better results than random sampling sampling, despite expected synergies. The principal obstacle to effective AL appears to be the inherent selection of an uneven class distribution, despite BASE's success with naturally balanced datasets. Our findings are accompanied by publicly available code on GitHub at the specified URL. 

Our BASE algorithm is straightforward and designed to be scalable for large, industrial applications. BASE generates a baseline for the evaluation of intricate AL algorithms in challenging, real-world settings. Our research provides a foundation for the exploration of novel AL methods and algorithms capable of addressing the key issues faced with existing AL algorithms. 

Our research concludes by highlighting the unmet challenges of AL in realistic scenarios and large-scale industrial settings. The code for BASE is intended to facilitate the development of a robust AL algorithm capable of addressing the inherent class imbalance issue and leveraging the benefits of self-supervised pretraining for a wide range of applications. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating interaction between these two levels was developed to explain the behavior observed in the larger samples. Furthermore, resistivity peaked at the neutral point in both sample types, and resisted increase with magnetic field strength due to a pinning effect caused by interaction between the two levels. This resulted in a magnetoresistivity curve with a resistivity spike at the neutral point, and a resistivity floor that increased with magnetic field. This pinning effect was found to lead to destruction of the resistivity spike at long measurement times due to gradual shift of the Landau levels with time. Consequently, formation of the resistivity spike depends on measurement time, with larger samples exhibiting the spike more frequently due to their larger neutral state edge energy separation. This edge state behavior was observed over an 18-year period at one particular research site, and has only been replicated at locations with specific geological conditions. This suggests that formation of the resistivity spike is influenced by local geoelectric conditions, and may be related to presence of certain crystallographic facets, as well as factors like snow cover and temperature. Consequently, this phenomenon is considered rare and unique to certain sites with particular magnetic field conditions, making it challenging to study. This investigation contributes to ongoing discussion on unique transport properties of HgTe quantum wells, and edge state behavior in the presence of a magnetic field. This has implications for understanding behavior of other two-dimensional materials with direct bandgaps, and provides a framework for a model that explains interaction between the neutral state at the edge and the non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Furthermore, our approach can be adapted to incorporate various constraints and scheduling modes, making it a versatile and dynamic TDD scheduling solution.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. We attribute the improved performance to the precise nature of gradient estimates provided by the ODE network. Additionally, we observe the distinctive ability of our Hamiltonian Neural Network to pick up on the underlying dynamics of the artificial task and replicate them in the meta-learning phase, as shown through the accurate recovery of the optimal trajectory for a hypothetical state in the artificial task. Moreover, our model exhibits a notable reduction in the number of forward passes required to reach this optimal trajectory, demonstrating its ability to identify and leverage the most crucial aspects of the artificial task, along with its underlying dynamics. We conclude that our approach provides a promising starting point for further exploration of the relationship between optimizers and the inductive bias inherent in machine learning models. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this reliability-enforcing mechanism is effective across various model types and does not significantly compromise the model's performance in tasks that prioritize prediction accuracy over precision. Our approach has the added benefit of enabling seamless integration with existing machine learning pipelines, making it a practical solution for enhancing the trustworthiness of machine learning models. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. In the process, we outline a more general construction for super-symmetric colored Jones polynomials on the torus. The discussion is accompanied by an executable mathematical content, encoded using the Computer Algebra System, SageMath. The associated code is designed to generate analytical and numerical data for various links, and is intended to support further research in the field. The development described in the paper has been made public on GitHub, at the address https://github.com/ConjectureDev/VolumeeConjectureDev. In the mentioned repository, findings for additional links can be viewed, and the project's framework is poised to contribute to future explorations of the volume conjecture. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the phase space for top quark production was expanded by investigating the characteristics of events containing one isolated electron or muon and three jets, from 163 inverse nanobarns of luminosity, and by establishing lower bounds on top quark pair and single-top quark cross-sectional areas of 36 and 11 nanobarns with 8-nanobarn uncertainties, respectively. These findings demonstrate the capability of the CMS experiment to study top quark production in heavy nuclear collisions and provide a foundation for further research into the properties of top quarks in these interactions. The results from the 2016 proton-lead run at the LHC were also compared with top quark production in proton-proton collisions at the same energy, finding that heavy nuclear collisions allow for the production of single-top quarks at a center-of-mass energy of 8.16 TeV, whereas in proton-proton collisions, such events are extremely rare. The most statistically significant set of single-top quark events to date was also presented, having been obtained from the 2017 proton-proton run at the LHC with a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV using a data set totaling 520 inverse nanobarns of luminosity, and the predicted characteristics of these events were found to be in line with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs along with their implications for GNNs. This exploration is accompanied by an examination of how different graph structures, such as acyclic graphs and trees, facilitate the application of GNNs in a private setting. Ultimately, our work is valued for its potential to guide future work aimed at integrating privacy and GNNs in an consistent and rigorous manner. This integration is crucial given the rising interest in graph-based machine learning, coupled with growing concerns about data privacy. As proof of concept, we developed a private training system for link prediction on knowledge graphs, demonstrating the practical applications of our analysis. This knowledge graph prediction dataset is an extension of the standard knowledge graph formation tasks known as WIKIDATA Large. It comprises a large dataset consisting of 9.5 million statements, 11 million edges, and 750 graph predicates. To evaluate our system, we constructed a smaller, more challenging version of this dataset, referred to as WL-Small. This dataset encompasses 1.5 million statements, 1.5 million edges, and 50 graph predicates. Notably, our approach is the first known attempt to incorporate privacy into GNNs when predicting relationships in knowledge graphs. This prediction task is challenging due to its extensive memory requirements, coupled with the need to develop a system that can handle extensive graph data while upholding high accuracy standards. This issue is further compounded by a lack of publicly available graph-based machine learning models trained on large-scale private datasets. This lack of availability is a major limitation faced by our approach, highlighting the need for future work aimed at addressing this shortage. Our approach leverages GNNs to predict relationships in knowledge graphs by conducting node representations updates based on a set of predefined rules. This representation update process is susceptible to various attacks that compromise the security of our approach. To mitigate this risk, we employed a private training system that combines GNNs

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Our results demonstrate that this stochastic hydrodynamic model effectively captures the dynamics of interacting Bose gases in non-equilibrium situations, and our approach provides a useful framework for studying such systems within the full quantum regime. This research paves the way for further investigations into complex non-equilibrium scenarios, including sound propagation in periodic potentials, as well as interacting Bose-Josephson junctions. Our findings are published in Physical Review X, and our simulations reveal that this regime is characterized by a novel regime of quantum shock wave propagation that is distinct from both classical and semi-classical regimes, and may give rise to unusual effects such as shock wave scattering off periodic potentials. This leads to an idea of a new quantum regime that can be experimentally probed by driving a system strongly off equilibrium, and comparing the outcomes to predictions made using the Bogoliubov approach. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. The approach used in the article involves employing the theory of relatively 1-homotopy classes to analyze a particular problem of minimal surfaces, and the results can be applied to demonstrate the convergence of a sequence of surfaces with minimal area in a given relative 1-homotopy class, without relying on the compactness theorem for minimal surfaces. This last application is then utilized to address the problem of showing that a sequence of surfaces with minimal area in a certain relative 1-homotopy class can be found within a bounded distance from a given surface, given that the area of the sequence's surfaces becomes finite as the index increases. This generalizes an important result due to G. Huisken and C. Conrad. The article's main ideas are further developed in the recent book "Minimal surfaces and the Lagrangian method" by C. Conrad. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, and more specifically between 2.0 to 3.5 MeV, where many excited states reside, were found to result from a competition between prolate and gamma shapes. This research revealed a unique and short-lived phase of shape coexistence in 64Ni, fueled by neutron pairs, and marked by an unusual relationship between the 0+4 and 2+1 states, that is distinct from the typical large energy gaps observed in other nuclei with shape coexistence. This extraordinary and fleeting phase of shape coexistence in 64Ni may be associated with a specific configuration that is highly sensitive to the effective Hamiltonian and effective interaction, and as such, represents a particular instance of shape coexistence that is not typically seen in nuclear physics. This research was made possible by a comprehensive understanding of the 64Ni nucleus gained from four separate experiments using different production methods and detection systems. This comprehensive knowledge base allowed scientists to reconcile any potential discrepancies in the data, that if analyzed separately, might have provided an incomplete picture of the 64Ni nucleus. This exceptional level of understanding was achieved using a combination of three methods: measuring the decay from the beta-proton decay of 64Cu, determining the levels of 64Ni through muonic X-rays following the reaction of 64Ni with 0.158 GeV protons, and finally, mapping the energy spectrum of 64Ni following the reaction of 100 mg 58Ni with 60 MeV alpha particles at the RIBF in Japan. This thorough analysis allowed scientists to establish a reliable and exclusive connection between the energies and spins of the excited states in the 64Ni nucleus, that is critical for understanding the underlying fundamental nuclear physics. This knowledge about the 64Ni nucleus has significant implications for predicting the properties of other Ni isotopes with similar characteristics. This research was an extensive collaboration between scientists from the United States, Europe, and Asia. This study was made possible by the cutting-edge capabilities of several world-class particle and nuclear physics facilities

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Experimental findings confirm that j-k fold CV yields superior performance compared to conventional methods, along with significant improvements in solution reproducibility and intuitive optimal parameter selections. Our study hopes to kindle discussion and spur further investigation into the inherent properties of machine learning models when evaluated via j-k fold CV, with a view to refining existing techniques and ensuring that model performance estimations are both highly reliable and accurate. To facilitate this goal, our research dataset is accessible online, featuring j-k fold CV assessments for diverse pre-trained LL models across 8 NLP tasks following 5, 10 and 20 fold CV schemes, along with corresponding model performance annotations. Consequently, fellow researchers can build upon our study by utilizing our pre-processed models, thus allowing for a concentrated examination into the fundamental characteristics of machine learning models in relation to performance estimation. Furthermore, our research provides actionable guidelines to support practitioners and machine learning model managers in implementing effective parameter tuning strategies, as supported by our empirical findings. Finally, our study suggests potential avenues for developing novel learning models that are inherently robust in the face of performance estimation variability, as highlighted by our empirical results. With this in mind, our research offers valuable contributions to the machine learning community at large. Our study's supplementary material is available online. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant FABE, which we found significantly enhances Bucket Elimination by substantially reducing the computational time and memory usage. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that become more noticeable as the angle between the atomic beam and the direction of the light increases. In our experiment, the effects of photon recoil were substantial, accounting for approximately one-tenth of the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. We also examined the impact of photon recoil on the absorption profile of a cloud of atoms when a cloud of atoms is exposed to a broad beam of light, and our results from this experiment matched predictions made by numerical simulations with an accuracy of approximately 10%. Our research revealed that the effects of photon recoil become even more significant when multiple beams of light are used in intersection, as seen in experiments like three-dimensional molecular reconstruction, yet our strontium experiment faced a limitation due to saturation effects even in a single-beam setup. Our findings are significant for experiments involving atomic or molecular beams and multiple-beam setups, and we believe they underscore the value of carefully evaluating absorption patterns in such experiments. In addition, we have made our numerical code available online for the benefit of the scientific community. This code can be utilized to simulate the absorption of light beams through clouds of atoms accurately, taking into account the recoil effects caused by the absorption and emission of photons. This knowledge is crucial for accurately interpreting data from experiments designed to reconstruct three-dimensional molecular information from multiple-beam experiments with ultracold atoms. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/ourpaper/code. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for exploring the relationship between the microscale interactions driving the shear thickening transition and the macroscopic phenomena observed in dense mixtures. Lastly, it highlights the intriguing connection between the point of shear jamming, the peak stress achieved during impact, and the role that microscale friction plays in this process. It is also noteworthy that the concept of shear jamming can be applied to various systems, including non-Newtonian fluids, granular materials, emulsions, and biologic tissues, making this research relevant to an broad and diverse range of scientific communities. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, a method for obtaining the veering triangulation associated with a loom space is presented, and it is shown that this process results in a loom space being reconstructible from its corresponding veering triangulation and root lamination. A significant finding in this context is the existence of a specific veering triangulation known as the central veering triangulation, which is derivable from every loom space and is distinguished by its unique, centrally located axis within the veering triangulation itself. It is also proved that the central veering triangulation is not only inherently linked to every loom space but also represents the most general form of veering triangulations linked to leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows. A final conclusion drawn from this research is that the core curve of a loom space can be obtained through an order-2 veering projection from its associated central veering triangulation, with this process being accompanied by a description of the resulting curve's topology. A notable connection between the central veering triangulation and the core curve of a loom space is established through its veering map, along with an exploration of the implications resulting from its order-2 nature. Furthermore, necessary and sufficient conditions for a veering triangulation to be classified as the central veering triangulation linked to a specific loom space are established, with these conditions also providing a framework for understanding the veering triangulations associated with order-2 veering projections on surfaces of genus two or higher. A final section is dedicated to a veering triangulation-linked surface of genus three, with this surface being characterized by a unique attribute: its associated veering triangulation exhibits an axis that is comprised of three distinct branches, while also being linked to an order-2 veering projection with unique properties. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This approach allowed us to estimate the drag experienced by the cylinder's flat ends with some accuracy, but was less effective for estimating the drag experienced by its sides. This approach also enabled us to explain the anisotropy we observed with the properties of the grains and the speed at which the cylinder was moved. This knowledge could be useful in a variety of contexts, including the cultivation of crops in soil and the development of underwater engineering projects. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These findings align with previous observations regarding $v_2$ and provide evidence for a similar phenomenon involving $v_3$. Furthermore, we re-examined the issue of spinodality's potential impact on $v_3$ and concluded that it holds a minor influence on current data. Our research also compared the results of our model to corresponding data from STAR and PHENIX collaborations, revealing overall agreement. Finally, we analyzed the role of initial random fluctuations and neutron star matter-like equation of state on $v_3$, determining their respective effects on $v_3/\epsilon_3$ within our model. This result is characterized by a unique relation that holds both locally and generally, offering potential utility for future reference. This research further delves into specific aspects of relativistic heavy ion physics, building upon our initial study, and contributes to the ongoing search for theoretical understanding of $v_3$. This knowledge may also be applied to future collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically the one involving Pb+Pb collisions at 13 GeV. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is implemented in the open-source software NGSolve, and its effectiveness is illustrated through numerical experiments on sample PDEs. Furthermore, the study provides a comprehensive analysis of its convergence properties. To facilitate widespread adoption, the proposed algorithm is designed to be easily integrable into existing solvers, and feature-rich software like NGSolve is an ideal platform for demonstrating the method's versatility. In particular, the study shows how to extend the proposed iteration to systems of nonlinear equations with multiple right-hand sides, and discusses the related challenge of infeasible systems of equations. Finally, the study acknowledges the widespread use of automatic differentiation as a primary approach for preserving intrinsic properties in numerical approximations. In contrast, the proposed iteration is positioned as a more efficient alternative, especially for large systems of equations, and one that can be easily integrated into existing solvers, albeit with a slight increase in the number of iterations required to achieve the desired level of precision. In conclusion, the proposed modification to the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration offers a promising solution for preserving intrinsic properties in time-dependent PDEs, especially those involving large systems of equations, and makes it suitable for widespread adoption in the numerical community. In addition, the associated algorithm is now available online as part of the NGSolve software package, and researchers are encouraged to test the proposed method with their own problems and models. In this regard, the developed software provides a convenient opportunity to experiment with the proposed method, and offers a markable step towards developing similar solvers for other PDEs.
