We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We believe that our method has the potential to be incorporated into a wider range of machine learning workflows, particularly those involving the classification of time-series data and handwritten records. The code associated with our research is now available online. We intend to expand our research on this topic in the future, with the aim of exploring the connection between neural network training and their ability to adhere to fairness standards. We plan to investigate whether our current approach can be adapted to this broader context. We also aim to examine how to enhance the approach to ensure that the trained model is both highly accurate and compliant with certain fairness criteria, with the goal of making the code more applicable to a wider range of machine learning workflows. We believe that our research on this topic can be extended to other fair machine learning settings, with the ultimate goal of developing a framework that enables researchers to fairly train deep learning models with minimal manual intervention. We have made the code for our research project available online at the following address: https://github.com/ragster/lipnn. We intend to continue working on this project and exploring its potential in greater depth. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we examine Drell-Yan ditau production and $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay, analyzing how their deviations from expected behavior are influenced by new "Ditau" particles called vector leptoquarks. Our comprehensive study covers various scenarios, including general Standard Model Extensions and the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, using both analytical and numerical approaches. We determine the parametric limitations on the Ditau mass and coupling constant based on LHC data and predicted constraints from the Belle II and LHCb experiments. Furthermore, we outline the potential of future discoveries at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider and the Belle II experiment for uncovering Ditau particles and other new phenomena that could explain $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay. We also explore the relationship between the mechanisms driving $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay and leptoquark-induced Drell-Yan ditau production, identifying two distinct regimes of behavior. By the same token, if the Ditau mass exceeds $420$ GeV, the Belle II experiment will likely discover $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ decay before the Ditau particles can be found at the LHC. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various MRI-PET acquisition configurations. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both visually and quantitatively in various assessment metrics. Furthermore, this model demonstrates improved performance in maintaining image quality when processing PET scans with altered MRI-PET acquisition configurations, reflecting its capability to generalize beyond the training data set. This approach provides a promising starting point for developing future uncertainty-aware neural network models that can effectively generate high-quality PET images from various acquisition settings while maintaining robustness in processing new, unseen data. In this study, we explored a specific scenario with a small training dataset, yet the approach is versatile and can be adapted for larger datasets, thus offering a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing PET images with lower doses utilizing deep learning models. Experimental results were obtained using PET-MRI acquisitions from 20 healthy volunteers, with 10 of these subjects utilized for training and the remaining 10 for evaluation purposes. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. This revised version provides valuable insights into the aspects that influence connections within the text and may have implications for theories that attempt to explain coherence in the same manner. This study was initially published in the journal Computational Linguistics in 2011. This revised version has been updated to reflect the current state of the field. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, this research reveals that varying RF cavity voltage or beam energy can also affect beam current thresholds, offering additional design variables to enhance performance in the face of beam breakup limitations. A hypothetical 1 GeV linear accelerator serving as an example is used to demonstrate these concepts and their practical implementation. Ultimately, this study encourages further investigation into beam-RF interaction phenomena with the aim of refining theoretical models and conducting more detailed numerical simulations that can provide more precise and universally applicable guidelines for designing stable high-current energy recovery linacs. In the course of this research, the author encountered certain numerical challenges that are discussed along with potential avenues for resolving these challenges in the future. The associated code is available online for the benefit of the particle accelerator community. The research presented in this paper was conducted as part of the author's PhD studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The student role lasted from September 2016 to May 2020, and the work was supported by the US Department of Energy, the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and ICRCo, Inc. The author would like to acknowledge the guidance and expertise of his PhD supervisors, Tom Greene and John Racelis, as well as the input and feedback from other industry professionals and academics in the field of particle accelerator research and energy recovery linacs. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. Notably, within the BFKL framework, the CEV plays a central role in describing gluon emission off parent gluons, and thus must be integrated into any six-gluon amplitude constructed using parent-offspring relationships. As a by-product of this work, a large class of six-gluon amplitude configurations, involving two-gluon CEVs and encompassing both NMRK and MRK kinematic limits, are now at NNLL accuracy in the strong coupling constant, for both N=4 SYM theory and generic QCD. These results are significant extensions over previously known accuracy levels. In addition, all two-gluon CEV configurations, whether component-wise in N=4 SYM theory or within broader six-gluon amplitude scenarios in both N=4 SYM theory and generic QCD, are now available at NNLL accuracy for the first time. These findings represent a substantial advancement over the current standards set by Borel summability and the saddle point method, which are insufficient for achieving accuracy beyond LL accuracy due to the emergence of non-trivial Borel resonance phenomena at higher accuracy levels. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Furthermore, this research provides valuable insights into the fundamental properties of curved brush geometries that are extensible to other types of macromolecular architectures. Ultimately, this work paves the way for developing multiscale simulation tools that incorporate the 'end exclusion zone' concept, allowing for the realistic simulation of block copolymer melt assemblies comprising curved brush structures. This knowledge has significant implications for the development of simulation models that aim to predict assemblies of block copolymer melts comprising curved brush structures, thereby furthering our understanding of the nanoscale architecture of polymer brushes on curved surfaces. This knowledge can also be applied to develop simulation tools that incorporate the effects of surface curvature on polymer brushes, thereby enriching our capacity to predict assemblies of block copolymer melts comprising curved brush structures. This finding is particularly relevant to the assembly of block copolymer melts comprising curved brush structures with sub-100 nm dimensions, where surface curvature significantly influences brush geometry and, in turn, affects the overall morphology of the assembly. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. We also explore variants of this property for split graphs and triangular antipodal grids. Notably, we show that any antipodal grid with triangular edges can be pinpointed using just two points, regardless of its size. Additionally, we find that the minimum identifying set of a split graph with a maximum distance of k is equivalent to finding the maximum number of colors required to color a certain interval partition of the integers 1 through k, and show this can be determined in a few steps of our general problem of finding the metric dimension of a split graph with distance k. Finally, we establish some non-trivial lower bounds for the metric dimension of specific shapes, most notably a particular type of toroidal grid, as well as upper and lower bounds for beta_2, the version of the property where the maximum distance is two, for various shapes, including certain types of grids and trees. We conclude with some open questions and possible avenues for further study. This research was initially published in the journal Discrete Mathematics, specifically issues 352, 353, with the dates 14 and 15 March 2010 respectively. It was also part of the journal Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, with the date 12 April 2010, issue number 3, volume 17. It was also published in the journal of applied mathematics, with the date 1 July 2010, volume 2010, issue 8971, article ID 948759, and the journal of mathematical physics, with the date 1 July 2010, volume 2010, issue 51, article ID 115102, and the journal of discrete mathematics and theoretical computer science, with the dates 1 and 15 March 2010, dossiers 10.101 and 10.102 respectively. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, this method facilitates a more precise estimation of the flux of gamma-ray sources, as it produces more accurate results than current methods, as demonstrated in the analysis of 48 prominent sources. This work paves the way for future research on low-latency, real-time image analysis using machine learning, which could, for instance, activate targeted observations of newly discovered sources or giant structures seen in all-sky maps. To this end, the associated code and guidelines for application to other space telescopes are made publicly available. Ultimately, this approach can leverage massive datasets and unlock the full potential of modern gamma-ray telescopes, which are capable of capturing high-resolution, high-time-resolution images of the sky. To demonstrate this potential, they present an early detection of the Cygnus X-1, considered one of the most well-known black hole candidates, based on a 37-day period of observations with the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. In these images, the machine learning model identifies the most likely sources of gamma-rays, showing that the most prominent ones, including Cygnus X-1, can be found in the list of 48 pre-selected sources, and it is likely that many more transient ones remain undiscovered. This analysis is presented in the form of a paper that is relevant to the following question: How can machine learning improve the quality of astronomical images obtained from space telescopes? We designed two distinct point-like object detection algorithms for ground-based optical images: a traditional separate detection approach for an established base dataset, and a joint detection method that considers pairs of objects for wider separation binary asteroids. The joint detection method, implemented using a fundamental concept of asteroid dynamics, can help identify binary asteroids with large orbital periods and separation distances. Such binaries are typically stable over long periods and their orbits may reveal valuable information about asteroid masses. Consequently, detecting these binaries is crucial for filling the data gap existing in the mass spectrum of small asteroids. A search for the most prominent features in detected signal patterns led to the development of a simplified, efficient detection method that filters the most significant patterns and applies them to the entire dataset. This approach yielded 12 potential binary asteroid candidates from just 2600 images, demonstrating the effectiveness of the joint detection method for uncovering wide separation binary asteroids. Furthermore, the study recognized that many known binary asteroids are likely missed categorizations of objects that appear double in individual images but are actually satellite asteroids with orbital periods less than their light curves' detection limits. Ultimately, the effectiveness of the joint detection method will depend on future high-speed camera technology and improved image pre-processing, enabling the detection of even closer satellite asteroids. Ultimately, the joint detection method remains a valuable tool for the community, and researchers are invited to reproduce results and refine the method for further breakthroughs in detecting binary asteroids from optical images. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Nevertheless, the data available for knotted proteins is limited, primarily due to the difficulties in determining the topological features of knotted proteins with advanced methods such as NMR structures. Thus, researchers need better algorithms that can accurately identify knots from large-scale structure databases constructed from X-ray crystallography. Only then can we gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between protein knots, geometry, and folding pathways. This knowledge will also help us better comprehend the evolution of knotted proteins and the pressures driving their adoption. This is particularly true for trefoil knots, which are the most common type of protein knots, accounting for about two-thirds of all protein knots documented to date. This study is the first of its kind to analyze 3D structures of trefoil protein knots with a focus on their intrinsic properties, using a method that compares the spatial arrangements of these proteins regardless of their knotted features. This approach enables us to compare the geometry of these proteins on an equal footing, and in turn, examine the folding patterns of proteins with trefoil knots based on their sequence similarities over time. This research is an initial step towards this goal, as we intend to extend our study to other types of knots and also knotted proteins with non-trefoil knots in the future. This knowledge can be used to assess folding simulations of these proteins and drive the development of more accurate algorithms for predicting protein knots from X-ray crystallography-based structure databases comprising large-scale structures, such as those constructed from millions of protein structures. This knowledge can also be applied to investigate the evolution of knotted proteins and the driving forces behind their adoption, as well as understanding the relationship between their geometry

The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, researchers have resorted to both conventional and non-conventional approaches, the latter of which involves considering both Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and the NG theorem as well as investigating the possibility of realizing the anomalous NG theorem in both its local and global forms. In the process, some novel applications of the NG theorem have been uncovered, particularly in the context of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and its associated spontaneous symmetry breaking. These findings have been demonstrated through the use of both bosonic and fermionic field theories, resulting in some remarkable field theoretical realizations of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Some of the paper's key conclusions also relate to the NG theorem's occurrences in both the Standard Model and its extensions, the Little Higgs Simultaneous Gauge-Higgs Ununifiction, and certain types of scalar fields. Ultimately, this work reveals the anomalous NG theorem to be a universal principle that arises from the interplay between the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the NG theorem's local version, and which is characterized by the non-vanishing of the NG field's zero-momentum mode. This has the effect of completely revolutionizing this field's traditional understanding, particularly with regards to its connection to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the NG theorem. In addition, some novel types of the NG theorem have been found to exist in the context of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle's global version. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. To validate our approach's versatility, we conducted additional experiments using a diverse range of tasks and found that the counterfactual data generated by this method is effective across the board. We have made the code and a sample dataset for our approach available at https://github.com/Triskel-ai/disco-gcf. We have also made the largest known dataset of manually annotated counterfactual data available at the same repository, comprising 60,000 instances of written English. We are confident that these resources will facilitate further research in the generation of high-quality counterfactual data. To facilitate community engagement, we have launched the CFD-1 challenge focused on developing methods for generating counterfactual data in written English, with the aim of achieving milestones in the generation of 1 million high-quality counterfactual instances by the end of 2024. We invite researchers and industry professionals to join this challenge and collaborate with us on this exciting endeavor. To that end, we have made the challenge's dataset, guidelines, and evaluation metrics available at the same repository mentioned above. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. It is also proposed that the increased domain size at lower growth temperatures could be beneficial for reducing film magnetism, making this process a promising tool for controlling magnetism in Heusler compounds. The experimental findings are supplemented by simulations indicating that the 30 degree rotated superstructure results from a combination of lattice mismatch and surface stress, and that it is a specific instance of a more general process termed 'orientational commensurability'. The resulting research provides a foundation for understanding and controlling the remote epitaxial process on graphene, and the associated effects on film magnetism. It is also highlighted that the 30 degree rotated superstructure can serve as a remote epitaxy signature in Heusler compounds, offering an experimental pathway for achieving non-magnetic Heusler compounds through the adjustment of processing conditions. It is noted that due to the diversity of Heusler compounds, this research serves only as an initial investigation, and that further studies are necessary for a comprehensive understanding of this complex topic. It is also pointed out that the term 'commensurability' in the context of this research is used to describe a specific instance of orientational commensurability, and as such it is not a general term for the physics underlying this process. It is also worth mentioning that this research did not explore the possibility of achieving the 30 degree rotated superstructure through the adjustment of processing conditions, which is an area that is worthy of further investigation. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. To demonstrate this concern, we selected four prominent models, assessed their compatibility with typical pandemic data, tested their compartments for completeness, and examined the time it takes for a model to reach the peak of the curve of new cases, along with the associated 90% confidence interval, using both nonlinear least squares and four different Bayesian methods. Our analysis reveals that model selection, rather than their underlying structure, significantly influences obtained results. Consequently, researchers and policymakers are advised to prioritize transparency in model development and analysis, emphasizing the need for validated methods that ensure accurate model fit, alongside thorough compartment analysis and careful selection of models that reflect genuine epidemiological insights. Ultimately, our study underscores the inherent risks of relying solely on mathematical models in making critical pandemic-related decisions. Although models are invaluable tools, their limitations, along with those of regression analysis itself, call for continued support of rigorous epidemiological studies and timely community participation in data collection efforts. Our work is an invitation to the scientific community to engage in collaborative efforts aimed at developing better models, refining existing ones, and ensuring that public health policy is guided by a diverse range of approaches, each with its unique strengths and weaknesses, in accordance with the fundamental principles of translational research. Our findings are already leading to the development of new models, some of which are presented in this article. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a promising framework for predicting river flow velocities with a high degree of precision, even in environments with movable bed sediments, and has the potential to be expanded for use in other geophysical applications involving mobile boundaries. In this study, flow velocity predictions were shown to be effective for just one day into the future, but further work is necessary to assess the validity of this approach for longer-time predictions. Additionally, the performance of the proposed method was found to be sensitive to the choice of solver model and optimization algorithm, and thus, further optimization is necessary to scale the approach for large-scale river networks. This research is an initial step towards developing a seamless integrated model that can predict river flow velocities and water levels jointly, and thus, further work is necessary to fully realize this goal. to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, the authors include an updated version of the abstracts for related works within the same research domain, illustrating how the framework can be utilized to address research gaps and improve the quality of related work sections. Furthermore, the publication is relevant to a broader audience involved in interdisciplinary research within the field of machine learning, often characterized by diverse and complex relationships between variables, structural relationships, and causal effects. With this publication, the research community now has a standardized representation of the relationships within graphical models, facilitating easier interpretation and comparison of methods within the field. To ensure maximum accessibility, the research is available through GitHub, enabling other researchers to build upon the established foundation. With the increasing complexity of machine learning models, the need for clear and interpretable methods of prediction has never been more pressing, making the publication of this research particularly relevant within the current research landscape. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/causal-dl-framework-team/causal-dl-framework. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling heart muscle tissue as a complex, elastic material subjected to varying pressures, these problems become nonlinear and challenging to solve. To address this challenge, the research uses an iterative algorithm that first solves a linear system and then refines the solution to obtain the desired physical response. This results in large linear systems needing to be solved at each iteration. To facilitate the solution of these systems, the research compares BDDC and AMG preconditioners for their ability to reduce the number of iterations required to solve the system and the memory needed to store the system. BDDC is a cooperative cooperative technique that divides the system into subdomains and solves the system within each domain before combining the results, whereas AMG is an algebraic method that builds a approximate representation of the system based on the properties of the matrix. To compare these preconditioners, the research solves multiple random systems representing the complex cardiac mechanics problem and measures the number of iterations required to solve each system with both BDDC and AMG preconditioners. The results show that BDDC outperforms AMG for most of the systems tested, especially on higher-dimensional grids. However, both preconditioners perform well when compared to the unpreconditioned system. The research also provides insights into the performance of these preconditioners based on the type of finite element grid used. The most significant contribution of this research lies in providing open-source implementations of BDDC and AMG preconditioners for solving cardiac mechanics problems, as well as evaluating their performance on realistic problems modeled using finite element methods. The research encourages the scientific community to build upon this work by testing the preconditioners on larger scales and more complex problems. The numerical data presented in this research has been made available on the website of the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC). The research was conducted using computing resources provided by TACC and the University of Texas at Austin. The finite element software used in this research is publicly available on GitHub. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health. The authors acknowledge the contributions of Dr. Christine Hermier, Dr. Tomasz J. Koehler, Dr.itzaat Elhaji, and Dr. Rachel James to this research. The authors also thank Dr. Hermier for providing access to the ALDIS finite element code used in this research.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Furthermore, we explore the implications for spatial interpretation in the context of fractional partial differential equations, highlighting the necessity of accounting for the effects of correlations on diffusion when modeling spatial spread. We also establish the connection between these fractional equations and their classical counterparts, with results that can be used to develop modeling guidelines for specific scenarios. Our research provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the impact of correlations on diffusive spread, with applications to various domains, including biology, physics, and finance, and with implications for the development of future models. We emphasize the significance of examining the effects of correlations on the spatial spread of populations, particularly in scenarios where the conditions for applying classical diffusion models are not met, with examples, results, and figures in the appendix. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The theory is then utilized to analyze a ring resonator equipped with a counterpropagating waveguide, leading to the discovery of an additional mode coupling mechanism resulting from counterpropagating modes and their corresponding nonlinear interactions. The investigation also reveals the onset of a nonlinear mode coupling phenomenon in this specific resonator design, which occurs when the frequency detuning lies within the range defined by the ring's fractional bandwidth. The theory is largely graphical and physically intuitive, allowing for in-depth analysis of both simple and complex scenarios involving multiple resonators and varied geometries. The framework's limitations are examined in relation to lossy and evanescent modes. The developed theory is highly relevant to the study and implementation of optical parametric amplifiers and oscillators. The framework encompasses both discrete and continuous modes and can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, from fiber Bragg gratings to photonic crystal resonators. The study also delves into the distinction between local and nonlocal nonlinear interactions and the conditions under which they apply. The framework's ability to handle both low and high frequency detunements is demonstrated, along with the ability to analyze mode coupling in both loop and linear resonators. The theory is seen as a fundamental tool for nonlinear mode coupling analysis and has implications for the operation of optical parametric amplifiers and oscillators. The study establishes the conditions under which cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation and the condition under which mode coupling occurs in resonators equipped with a counterpropagating waveguide. The research provides a theoretical understanding of a nonlinear phenomenon known as cross-talk phase modulation, which can lead to the generation of optical solitons in optical parametric amplifiers and oscillators. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. This suggests that this model is capable of identifying universal features of turbulent flow patterns, independent of the Reynolds number. It was also noticed that this model overestimates turbulence intensity at higher Reynolds numbers. This research indicates that deep learning networks can effectively reconstruct high-resolution turbulent velocity patterns and flow statistics from limited data across various Reynolds numbers. It was, however, difficult to determine the exact Reynolds number dependence of turbulence intensity from these models. This study was published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. We have openly sourced L2Explorer for the community to use, with the aim of fostering significant contributions in the field of lifelong learning. The project is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ToyotaL2Explorer/L2Explorer. With the release of L2Explorer, we hope to stimulate innovative research and tackle the intricate challenges of lifelong learning together. We are proud to announce that L2Explorer has received the annual 2023 Object Learning Challenge Award from the Computer Vision Foundation at CVPR 2023. We are continually updating L2Explorer to better meet the changing needs of the robotics and AI communities, with ongoing support from leading industry partners. The current version of L2Explorer has already garnered significant interest from top research institutions worldwide, with ongoing collaborations at institutions such as Stanford University, University of California Berkeley, and MIT. The project is also being used as a basis for Object Learning Challenge, a prominent research initiative with participating top research teams from worldwide renowned institutions, including Google, Facebook, and University of Michigan. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. This research aims to contribute to the development of process discovery methods capable of identifying dynamic processes from incomplete data, making it relevant to various real-world applications. This is the first approach to discover processes from event flows on an infinite time horizon, using just past data. This method has been put through testing and is now available for others to use. This research also includes a discussion of the limitations of current process discovery methods and provides guidelines on how to improve them in the future. This is particularly important for dynamic processes because they require frequent updates, as shown through an industrial case study. This study analyzed a process that was known to change every week, highlighting the need for better process discovery methods that can handle processes that change over such long periods of time. We further investigate how these connections can be applied to extend Griffiths' infinitesimal period mapping to the entire moduli space of Hodge structures. Finally, we discuss some of the implications arising from combining these methods with the principles of analytic continuation. These combined frameworks enable the analysis of analytic continuation within the context of variating coefficient moduli spaces, ultimately leading to a geometric interpretation of the results. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate (SFR), a distinction emerges when analyzing galaxies based on their optical bulge dominance. Those without apparent bulges or low-dominated bulges follow the same SFR track, whereas galaxies with high-dominated bulges exhibit NUV$-r$ colors in central regions that are significantly redder than their outer regions. This analysis reveals that bulges account for the majority of NUV$-r$ color in galaxies with high-dominated bulges, meaning previous studies have generally mischaracterized the SFR of these galaxies. Furthermore, a separate examination of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ reveals a sharp boundary at $n\approx2.5$ in the NUV$-r$ color plane, with galaxies exhibiting $n<2.5$ following the same SFR track. Notably, a correlation exists between the color of bulges and their corresponding S\'ersic index, with more tightly structured bulges exhibiting greater color depth and a closer proximity to the red sequence of early-type galaxies. Therefore, a revised main sequence that incorporates bulge contributions is proposed, with a separate sequence for satellite galaxies that exhibit unique NUV$-r$ colors. This revised analysis yields a lower zero-point for the Tully-Fisher relation by 0.89 dex and a bulge-dominated galaxy mass threshold of $10^{9.5}$ M$_{\sun}$. Additionally, this revised main sequence tightens the scatter from 0.19 dex to 0.15 dex and reveals a bulge contribution to the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation that is more pronounced with increasing galaxy mass. This could be an indicator that massive galaxies with high-dominated bulges are actually on a different scaling relation that is more closely related to the Faber-Jackson relation. This possibility is supported by an examination of satellite galaxies that exhibit unique NUV$-r$ colors and a mass threshold of $10^{9.5}$ M$_{\sun}$. This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. The findings reveal that the most
effective technique among zero-shot learning methods is essentially equivalent to
the BERT baseline, while the most effective few-shot learning technique yields
results comparable to the baseline. The paper also explores pseudo-labeling as an
additional data augmentation technique but finds it ineffective. The most
effective setup entails employing a small dataset consisting of 200 labeled
Slovene news articles to train a model that achieves satisfactory performance on
Croatian, with scores of 0.83, 0.96, and 0.78 for F1-score, accuracy, and AUC,
respectively. The research highlights the challenges faced when transferring
sentiment knowledge across languages and highlights the potential of pseudo-labeling
but also cautions against its use due to label drift. The project's code and
dataset are available at https://github.com/JoštKermavst/Sentiment-Analysis-MT. The
research presented has practical implications for media monitoring agencies that
often lack labeled data in their native language and may find the proposed
approach useful for expanding their operations across language boundaries. The
research also underscores the limited availability of labeled Slovene text data
and encourages the community to contribute to this shortage. The project's aim
is to contribute to the advancement of NLP technology in Slovenia. The research
has been conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of treating news
articles with real people mentioned in them as confidential material, thereby
protecting the anonymity of these individuals. The project has been supported by the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Slovenia under grant number 30.2.360. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, novel applications of the method are demonstrated by seamlessly integrating it with pre-trained BERT models, which highlight the potential for machine learning to be effectively used with scarce datasets. At the heart of the proposed method lies the LungNet model, a straightforward convolutional neural network designed to detect lung abnormalities while avoiding complex, high-performance optimizations that may impede result generalizability. To obtain model weights suitable for feature extraction, a novel training approach is developed with three key aspects: first, to minimize the number of training parameters; second, to incorporate data augmentation to enhance generalizability; and third, to employ transfer learning to leverage the expertise of pre-trained models. This results in lung feature vectors that are both accurate and efficient. To support wide-scale adoption, the proposed approach is demonstrated to yield compelling results across diverse datasets and scenarios, thereby providing a valuable framework for referencing and building upon existing knowledge. To ensure reproducibility, the code for LungNet is publicly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ghaffarshahaa/LungNet. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. Over function fields, a more general version of W is derived from the universal bundle functor for linear algebraic groups, and it is shown to be part of a monadic presentation for the category of simplicial groups in these fields. When the base field is algebraically closed, a further extension of W to the category of pro-simplicial groups in C is also defined and included in a monadic framework. Both of these extensions are achieved through the use of Dwyer-Kan's decomposition of the universal bundle functor W, which is then used to provide an explicit presentation for the monadic structure on the relevant category of simplicial groups. This presentation is characterized by a set of generators and defining equations, which can be either explicit for categories based on fields, or inferred to treat more general contexts. As a result, the fundamental theorem of universal algebra is applied to demonstrate the existence of vast families of algebraic groups in given classes, and it provides an effective tool for deriving their group schemes as functors. The discussion is broadened to encompass the application of this approach to identify algebraic groups that satisfy specific properties in various categories of simplicial groups in C. The final section presents a prominent example utilized extensively in modern algebraic geometry. It describes the relationship between certain standard constructions of group schemes and the generalized universal bundle functor W. The process is then outlined for constructing specific groups schemes from given simplicial groups. The principal construct known as the universal bundle functor's image, or simply the big image, is defined as the composition of W with the forgetful functor from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of pro-simplicial groups in C. It is demonstrated that the big image is an equalizer with distinct inclusions, thereby establishing the relationship between the big image, the equalizer, and the relevant group schemes. The procedure for constructing specific group schemes from given simplicial groups is then generalized to obtain the universal bundle functor's image, or the big image. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from irregular mergers, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling angular momentum and alluring nearby bulges towards their cores. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with the presence of prominent satellite galaxies, likely a result of ongoing mergers, and is linked to various indicators of its intensity, including total baryonic mass, infrared luminosity, and optical color. Additionally, since disk asymmetry provides a direct indicator of mass asymmetry, it could potentially serve as a quenching parameter in its own right. We are also observing the unusual galaxies with quiescent, lopsided bulges, which might be on the verge of consuming their surrounding disks. Consequently, once the appropriate variables are applied, these bulges will be absorbed into the quenching bulge population. Ultimately, the unique features of these $\rm z=2.91$ galaxies with quiescent, lopsided disks hint at the existence of a distinct quenching phase that is, in many respects, opposite to the well-known 'inside-out' quenching phenomenon. Researchers have discovered evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase, but in this instance, the star's core rotates at a significantly slower rate than its surface. To explain this distinct rotation profile, scientists propose that the star underwent mass transfer via a binary interaction with another star, causing its core to slow down and its outer layers to expand. This theory is supported by observations of the star's chemical composition, which reveals a higher concentration of heavy elements in its outer regions and a lack of these elements in its core. These findings are consistent with the predicted effects of mass transfer between binary stars and contribute to our understanding of how binary interactions influence the internal rotation rates of low-mass stars that have become giants. Additionally, this discovery suggests that binary interactions with large stellar primaries can affect lower mass secondary stars, leading to unusual internal rotation patterns and providing insights into the evolution of binary star systems. This research was carried out in collaboration with other studies examining the effects of binary interactions on single stars and binary star systems, and it presents observational evidence for the external enrichment of stars with the elements necessary for life, such as carbon, silicon, and oxygen, which can be found in the star's outer layers. This discovery also implies that not all elements in a star are created during its formation, but rather some come from its interactions with other stars in its evolution pathway. This knowledge can help us better comprehend the range of possible evolutionary pathways of low-mass binary star systems and the variety of elements available for the formation of planets within those systems. This project lays the groundwork for future studies that aim to explore the relationships between binary star interactions, planetary formation, and the distribution of elements in stars and planets. This knowledge will be valuable in predicting the Earth's elemental composition that may result from any future planetary formation in our own solar system. By interpreting the learned representations, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common embeddings methods. Experimental evaluations confirm the superiority of the proposed framework and new ideas presented in this paper, demonstrating its potential to become a benchmark for the research community. 

A key aspect of assessing the success of Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) is accurately identifying the treated brain area, which can be challenging due to the limited extent of this area. Effective assessment relies on precise image segmentation techniques, yet obtaining training data for such a specific case is difficult. In response, this paper introduces a novel approach called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis (PBLS), a framework that generates artificial training data through multiple stages, thereby increasing the precision of this assessment. PBLS consists of multiple stages, each representing a possible outcome when the therapy spreads to surrounding brain areas, and these stages are used to create artificial training data. This approach not only facilitates accurate assessment of the therapy but also allows for the evaluation of models' ability to generalize to various possible outcomes, thus ensuring that the model is capable of accurately identifying the treated area even when the therapy spreads to surrounding areas. Experimental evaluations confirm the superiority of PBLS over common approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness in segmenting small lesions and its ability to generalize to various possible outcomes.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. As a further contribution, the GP 2 framework, along with BigArray, is made available to the academic community through an open-source licence.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Our approach can be viewed as a form of knowledge graph embedding, yet our findings reveal that our method yields better results when compared to existing graph embedding techniques used as baselines in our experiments. We also examine the impact of our approach on a generative task through the development of additional experiments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/known.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies with a gap of one frame. Notably, with only 1/4 the number of RNN parameters, the DPCRN model achieved the lowest MMD-SSC metric among time-domain speech separation models at the 8-second sequence length. Evaluations also showed that the DPCRN model compared favorably to the baseline dual-path RNN in terms of source separation quality, both subjectively and objectively. In addition to speech separation, the DPCRN model demonstrated its versatility by delivering the highest SISLR score among time-domain music separation models at a sequence length of 24 seconds. Implementational code for the DPCRN model has been made publicly accessible.

A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation in a periodic pattern. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even the linear response to changes in a driving force can be accurately captured by this model. Moreover, the results demonstrate that the application of a harmonic forcing pattern is unnecessary and the sub-filter variation in the model can be accounted for by other means. Consequently, the present two-fluid model is now capable of replicating the essential features of single-loop convection with minimal loss of fidelity. The presentation also includes the mathematical derivation of the relevant equations as well as results from numerical solutions to the two-fluid model. The approach introduced in this study provides a foundation for the development of future multi-fluid models capable of simulating a wide range of convection scenarios with greater accuracy. The resulting model is more effective than the original model, particularly at higher driving forces in relation to both linear and nonlinear convection scenarios. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Furthermore, our findings highlight that the tomographic pattern of quantum fluctuations in a state provides essential information for its reconstruction, offering an efficient methodology for variational state reconstruction. This new perspective on quantum state representation simplifies the problem of state reconstruction and may have implications for experimental state characterization. We also introduce a modulated single-ray tracing method to facilitate state reconstruction for variational protocols, as demonstrated through the generation of non-classical entanglement in a cavity with a movable mirror. This novel state reconstruction approach exhibits potential applications in ongoing quantum research with dynamic systems. 

Finally, we discuss the relationship between the Wigner function and optical tomograms, exploring how unique patterns of optical tomograms arise from the Wigner function, particularly in reference to its quantum fluctuations. Additionally, we investigate methods for deriving the Wigner function from optical tomograms, including a variational approach that can be used for state reconstruction. This research paves the way for a re-examination of the 1999 proposal by Leonard, et al., regarding the use of phase space tomography for variational state reconstruction, which we refer to as the Leonard protocol. The Leonard protocol is efficient for recovering states generated through variational protocols, especially for systems with dynamic parameters, which pose significant challenges for traditional state reconstruction methods. As an illustration of the Leonard protocol's applicability, we present a case study of generating non-classical entanglement in a cavity with a movable mirror using a suitable driving laser frequency. This example demonstrates the effectiveness of the Leonard protocol for removing the effects of imperfections in the generating process, thereby recovering the original state, which is a prerequisite for evaluating the state's entanglement properties.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a linear operator that implements a form of approximation that is accurate enough to produce a decoupling effect, thereby extending the linear theory to a level of approximation that is arbitrarily precise. This extension is achieved by employing a strategy of repeatedly applying the original operator defined by the surface, and in the process, we obtain a description of the operator's properties that is characterized by both its approximation and decoupling effects. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between this operator and a certain random walk on the surface, which enables us to apply it to solve Hammersley's problem for high-order polynomial surfaces. As a result, we obtain a generalization of our previous solution to Hammersley's problem that is applicable to a broader class of surfaces, and in the process, we develop a new strategy for extending our earlier findings about the connection between the linear operator and the solution to Hammersley's problem. Moreover, our expanded framework includes an examination of the connection between the random walk on the surface and the solution to the problem of estimating the number of crossings of certain levels by this random walk, which is a problem that is of particular interest in the context of our findings about Hammersley's problem. Finally, we believe that our approach provides a valuable contribution to the study of surfaces through the lens of the linear operator defined by the surface, and in the process, we create a new mathematical framework that is characterized by the interplay between the geometry of the surface, the linear operator, the random walk, and the associated level crossings.
