Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces output. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is shown to influence its ranking in the network's softmax probability distribution. This leads to the black-box knowledge distillation algorithm using the network's predictive ratings, which can be any score function that rates the input according to the decision it has made. A model trained using this method is found to match the performance of one trained using traditional knowledge distillation. The proposed approach is also shown to be highly effective in transferring knowledge from networks with different decision-making properties, such as those that make decisions based on softmax probability distributions and those that do not. This results in a more scalable deep learning framework where models can be easily stacked on top of each other, making it suitable for a wide range of computer vision tasks. The code for the study is available at https://github.com/ghyi/DBBKD. The proposed black-box knowledge distillation approach achieves state-of-the-art knowledge distillation performance, as demonstrated by its placement on the knowledge distillation leaderboard alongside current approaches that often yield superior results but require access to the original network. The study's findings are relevant to several applications involving deep neural networks, including computer vision tasks such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. The proposed method extends beyond these tasks to any problem that involves transferring knowledge between different models, even when access to the underlying workings of the source model is limited. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two agents in a cooperative learning environment via agent-agent imitation. Although agent agents can make mistakes, our method ensures they learn from each other's successful data sets by maintaining separate success buffers and employing them to train imitation learning models in an alternating manner. Successful experiences are defined as receiving a reward above a pre-determined threshold in our demonstration-intensive benchmark – Multi-Agent Walking. Our results indicate that using only 20% of the data used in traditional methods, CoIL is capable of achieving comparable performance. Moreover, CoIL outperforms methods utilizing extensive demonstrations in reinforcement learning in three other domains – Cart-Pole, Mountain Car, and Acrobot – by an average of 50% in terms of data efficiency. Our findings validate the efficacy of our Co-Imitation Learning framework in reducing the necessity for extensive demonstrations in various settings. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ghulamelfan/CoIL. Our research provides a foundation for exploring extensions to the basic agent-agent cooperation learning approach presented here. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. We conclude that search-limited PAC codes offer a compelling compromise between polar codes and conventional convolutional codes, with a further explored application in hybrid architectures. A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Our research also demonstrates the equivalence of (Np/q)d to the set defined by a specific context-free grammar, indicating that the recognisable subsets of (Np/q)d comprise a context-free language. Our contribution towards understanding the computational properties of base p/q systems provides a context for the discussion on the relationship between computation theories and number systems. Our research on base p/q systems expands upon the findings from our previous studies on base systems with irrational numbers. Our results demonstrate the limitations of base p/q systems when attempting to evaluate specific relationships, thereby highlighting the significance of the relationship between computation theories and number systems with an unbounded domain. Our research on base p/q systems also delves into the computational properties of systems based on rational numbers with an irrational extension, providing an interesting connection to the field of computability theory. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To demonstrate this efficiency, we developed a checker for a specific variant of snapshot isolation that is applicable to MongoDB's replica set deployment, and showed that this checker is significantly faster than a general-purpose checker for snapshot isolation. Our work provides a transparent and verifiable implementation of MongoDB's transaction protocols for each deployment scenario, and contributes to the broader field of distributed databases by highlighting the importance of formally verifying the consistency guarantees provided by modern NoSQL databases. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to the verification of other distributed database systems that offer similar consistency guarantees. Our checker for the replica set deployment is also a useful tool that can help database administrators identify potential issues with their MongoDB deployments. To facilitate further work in this area, we publicly released the pseudocode and checker for MongoDB's transaction protocols on our project website. Our research was motivated by the growing reliance on complex database systems and the need for rigorous methods to ensure the correctness of these systems in the wild. Our approach builds upon existing verification techniques for distributed systems, but diverges from them by focusing on the verification of the consistency guarantees provided by database systems rather than their overall behavior. Our work also involves a level of complexity that goes beyond typical NoSQL database systems, due to its inclusion of a specific system, MongoDB, and the development of a checker to identify potential issues with real-world deployments of this system. Our research was supported by the National Science Foundation, under grant number 1944286. Our approach has been designed to be adaptable for other distributed database systems that offer similar consistency guarantees, and our checker can be modified to accommodate these systems. Our research involved collaboration with database administrators from leading technology companies, including Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, who provided valuable insights into the verification of the consistency guarantees provided by these systems in real-world scenarios. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, giving rise to an intriguing interplay of geometry-driven frustration and ordering. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observed how the shift from local order to disorder is influenced by the level of frustration, which in turn affects network resilience in response to the removal of connections. Additionally, a newly Lees-Yang theorem-inspired analysis revealed an unexpected distribution of probabilities linked to the disorder state, which the authors believe can be applied more broadly to similar network disorders. Numerical data was validated using extensive simulations and variants of the model, opening up possibilities for applying these findings to diverse real-world applications. The model's unique blend of simplicity and representativeness makes it an engaging example of a non-equilibrium phase transition occurring within a complex network, steeped in real-world relevance. The underlying mathematical structure can be extended to incorporate more sophisticated triangle interactions, enabling further exploration of the interplay between geometry, frustration, order, and disorder. We studied the variation of solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also calculated the total solar wind energy flux for the same periods of time, which worked out to about 1.8 times ten to the power of twenty Watts, but with a margin of error, and this is consistent with the energy flux we could calculate directly from the data for the four individual approaches to the sun. One interesting point is that the solar wind energy distributions showed some slight humps or shifts in location, but only during the periods right around the equinoxes, but we couldn't rule out the possibility that these patterns could be the result of random fluctuations. We also looked at the characteristics of the solar protons in the wind, which showed some variation in terms of number, energy, and distribution, but these differences were not correlated with any particular features of the sun, but could have been the result of random fluctuations or possibly controlled by the Earth's magnetic field. We also considered the possibility that the protons could have originated from the tails of solar jets, but without more data, we couldn't say for certain. We did note that the energy flux of the solar protons was lower than would be expected based on the characteristics of the sun, but this could be the result of the protons being scattered in different directions by the magnetic field, but we needed more data to confirm this. We also found that the energy distributions of the electrons were similar to those of the protons, but the electrons showed some slight variation in location of the peak, but this could have been the result of random fluctuations.

Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Ultimately, the contribution of this work lies in providing a swift and precise approach to calculating hedging costs that can be readily employed in various existing models. The research underpins the development of more advanced projects, including an examination of the optimal hedging process and calculation of value-at-risk, both of which rely on the ability to efficiently determine hedging costs. The methodology introduced here can be extended to other types of European derivatives and complex hedging strategies. The associated software code is available on a relevant repository, inviting fellow researchers to build upon this work and explore related derivations. The research described in this paper was previously published in a 2023 date range, with the original research conducted under the guidance of Professor S. G. Krishna. The work discussed herein represents an expansion of the ideas presented in the earlier research, with the aim of sharing the expanded research with a broader audience. A higher education system or similar opportunities across generations can drive social mobility, but the relationship between education and mobility is more complex and depends on various factors including the system's accessibility and the economy. To study these dynamics, we developed a model that includes education as a key factor in status change, which we applied to an empirical analysis of data from the United States and Germany. Our results show that education is crucial for upgrading social status in both countries but has a limited impact due to significant barriers to entry. We also found that the effect of education on status change differs across different social classes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that while higher education can significantly improve employment prospects and income, it has a more moderate effect on reducing social status inequality compared to other factors like employment and income. Our study highlights the distinct challenges faced by the two countries in terms of social mobility and provides policy recommendations on how to improve education systems to enhance mobility. We propose that introducing more flexible education pathways and increasing funding could help improve education's effectiveness in upgrading social status. Our research demonstrates the value of an economic dynamics perspective in understanding social mobility and highlights the limitations of existing mobility measures by showing that income and employment are critical components of status change. Our empirical analysis in the appendix reveals that the German labor market has become significantly less responsive to education since the onset of the euro crisis, which we believe is an essential factor contributing to the lower mobility rates observed in Germany compared to the United States. Our study's policy implications emphasize the need for greater investment in education systems to enhance the chances of status upgrade for marginalized groups and the importance of creating more labor market opportunities that value education and skills equally across different social classes. Our empirical analysis also highlights the policy relevance of considering education's interaction with other factors of status change when analyzing and comparing the levels of social mobility in different countries. Our research's unique perspective on social mobility highlights the value of an economic dynamics approach that views social mobility as a continuous process of status change rather than a discrete event, and our results show that education is a critical component of this process but not a standalone determinant of social mobility. Our study's findings also underscore the challenges faced by developed economies in achieving high levels of social mobility and provide a framework for understanding the intergenerational persistence of social status. Our model's focus on ongoing status change through various channels offers a potential explanation for the notable social mobility observed in some developing countries. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits, providing critical input for particle beam dynamics simulations. A measure called "beam interaction point closeness" was also calculated to assess the consistency of beam closure within the 26.7 $\mu$m precision required for fulfilling physics production needs. Over the course of three years, over 1.5 million beam scans were conducted under regular operating conditions, using the CMS detector's muon spectrometer for beam closure mapping in the longitudinal direction. The successful implementation of emittance scans within the LHC's production schedule demonstrate their effectiveness and efficiency, and the developed techniques are now integral to the operation of the CMS experiment at the LHC. The implementation and experience gained from operating the CMS detector with the emittance scan technique will also be crucial for future upgrades and similar experiments at future lepton colliders. The method's validity has been validated through comprehensive simulations of post-shuffle beam properties and closed orbits with up-to-date LHC beam dynamics and CMS geometry. The technique's future potential has been assessed through the simulation of future LHC beam conditions and proposed lepton collider designs. The CMS experience serves as a model for other experiments at the LHC, and the technique has been made available to other LHC experiments. The emittance scan technique has been successfully utilized by the CMS experiment to meet its physics production needs, and it is anticipated that similar techniques will be crucial for future particle physics experiments at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). The technique's applicability to other contexts has been explored through the simulation of future LHC beam conditions and proposed lepton collider designs. The issue of beam-resonance occurrence during the course of experiments at the Large Hadron Collider was also addressed, alongside recommendations for optimal beam-tuning according to beam parameters and closed orbits. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. A comprehensive example is provided where the instrument in question is the next-generation CMB polarisation detector CMB-S4's Sunfish array at the South Pole, but the tool is designed to be highly adaptable for other experiments as well. A key aspect of's4cmb' is its ability to incorporate results from cosmological parameter estimation tasks that involve actual data sets, making it a valuable resource for the community at large. The code is accessible on GitHub and is intended to be utilized by the community with the hope of contributing to its development. The associated documentation is available on readthedown. To achieve this, we conducted additional tasks using the same data and refined the approach by carrying out automatic labeling. Our results show substantial improvements task-specific models achieve when leveraging TACKBERT compared to labeling individual sentences. We also investigate the effectiveness of different labeling strategies and other approaches like BART, which leads to a significant boost in performance. Further analysis of TACKBERT reveals that it draws upon background knowledge that it has been trained on, leading to some interesting patterns in the ordering decisions it makes. This is particularly evident when the task involves ordering sentences that are topically unrelated, yet it seems to employ a sensible order that mirrors general conversational flow. This is further illustrated by an example where we order sentences that are not technically related but follow a sequence of events in time, showing the potential for potential applications in areas like knowledge graphs and coreference. Our effort also highlights potential issues with the current Word Order Task setup, particularly the lack of explicit guidance on order relations, which we believe could significantly impact the task's difficulty. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our proposed method yields a notable 12.5% improvement in the accuracy of deepfake detection on Fawkes-resistant images obtained through the FaceForeniscs++ benchmark. Our implementation is available at this link: https://github.com/zhengyun113 MD-CSDNetwork.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the introduction of angle functions is equivalent to endowing spaces with a specific type of metric structure, thereby linking this concept to existing problems on metric spaces. Finally, the article presents an overview of the types of Euclidean spaces that can be obtained through the embedding methods discussed.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Ultimately, our research on Forsage serves as a starting point for further study of the vast array of pyramid scams that rely on blockchain technology. Our anonymous and publicly accessible research materials are available at [www.pyramidforge.com](http://www.pyramidforge.com). This research was made possible through the generosity of an anonymous donor who helped cover expenses related to its conduct. This work is a part of the broader project Securize Finance [www.securizefinance.org](http://www.securizefinance.org) that aims to empirically examine the workings of various scams and deceptive practices within the cryptocurrency industry. This project is dedicated to providing empirical knowledge about hidden transactions and shady business practices within the cryptocurrency sector, hoping to contribute to the development of more secure financial technologies. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.5 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160 which exhibited distinct movement patterns, potentially indicating a smaller satellite galaxy. We calculated their metallic content and ages; as expected, the metal content ranged widely from -1.8 to +0.5 and the ages ranged from 8 to 13 billion years with the exception of VVV-CL160 again which had a lower metal content and younger age. We further analyzed the possible presence of small satellite galaxies within the galaxy's bulge and the potential limitations of the current catalog of globular clusters. The research provides a comprehensive understanding of the galaxy's bulge's stellar population and the need for future observations of the proposed cluster candidates, particularly VVV-CL160. The findings also highlight the need for a revised and expanded catalog of the galaxy's globular clusters. The catalog of the galaxy's bulge clusters serves as a significant step in comprehensively understanding the galaxy's evolution and structure. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition of bright flare kernels and weaker ribbons in a larger area. This analysis also yields an excellent agreement with the semi-empirical EUVE flux spectrum of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, which was previously matched with a single-component beam model, but is now better explained by the two-component model, likely due to the larger size of that flare. This two-component electron beam model provides a useful framework for assessing the biosignatures on exoplanets in the habitable zones of low-mass stars with intense stellar flares, by considering the variability of UV flux in those planets' environments over time scales of years to decades. This variability could give rise to a biologically controlled counter-part, making the search for life on those planets more challenging, but also with new potential in detecting life that could resist extreme fluctuations in the environment. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, an abductive analysis of sparse coding's benefits is provided, along with the potential risks of using compact representations. To support broad applicability, the proposed SparseGAN architecture is adaptable across various generator models, including the standard GAN, Conditional GAN, and Vanishing GAN. An open-source implementation of the SparseGAN is available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/zuoyu2016/SparseGAN.

Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision. Our study provides valuable insights into the relationships among capture, recapture, and resource selection processes that underlie animal population dynamics.  These findings can be utilized to enhance the design of future studies involving capture and telemetry data, and inform researchers using related methods such as occupancy modeling. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy stress operator. The distinction between these two operators is the basis for an interesting discussion on the fundamental laws of mechanics governing closed systems, for which the Einstein operator is zero, whereas the Cauchy stress operator determines the configuration of these systems. The term "material operator" is introduced to describe the set of operators governing the dynamics of a system in relation to its material nature. The paper also delves into the connection between the Einstein operator, the Cauchy stress operator, and the Euler-Lagrange equation, highlighting how it arises from the variational principle of least action. The concept of the Einstein operator can be applied to any second-order differential equation defining a massive, free particle in D-dimensional space, leading to the discovery that the parameterization of these operators is deterministic and results in the Einstein operator being zero. The exploration of the Einstein operator is used as a starting point to examine the Cauchy stress operator on N-dimensional configuration manifolds, specifically in the context of variational problems involving extensive variables. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
This research provides a starting point for further exploration of nonparametric
traffic state estimation approaches.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Moreover, our results show that this method can be effective for developing wave extraction tools that rely on solutions to the Hamiltonian constraint. This approach has the potential to be a valuable addition to existing methods, given the variety of possible spacetime settings and matter configurations that can be tackled using this method alone. Our open-source code is specifically designed to be easily extensible for exploring other variants of this method. This approach can be applied to a range of scenarios, including but not limited to rotating black holes with axially symmetric perturbations, by employing appropriate boundary conditions to ensure that solutions satisfy axisymmetry and have specific polar symmetry. This method is particularly useful for producing high-accuracy solutions to the Hamiltonian constraint in scenarios involving fundamental fields, as it facilitates the recovery of field configurations from rescaled quantities, and it allows for the implementation of wave extraction tools that rely on solutions to the Hamiltonian constraint. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Notably, our results reveal that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN is approximately 0.053 $\mu$V/K, accompanied by a small anomalous Hall coefficient 0.083 $\mu$S/cm, indicating a substantial anomalous Nernst effect in this material, likely facilitated by its exceptional electronic conductivity and unique magnetic properties. Our study also highlights the anomalous Nernst effect's sensitivity to temperature and sample quality, emphasizing the necessity for high-quality materials and controlled experimental conditions when measuring this effect. Moreover, our findings provide a basis for understanding the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN relative to other materials, offering opportunities for exploring the anomalous transport properties in this class of materials. Our experimental approach can be applied to the study of the anomalous Nernst effect in other magnetic materials with clean and controlled samples, facilitating a deeper comprehension of the transport phenomena in transitional metal solids. We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles. These cocycles can then be used to map from ideals of K to torsion in rational groups of local Galois, thereby supporting the conjecture's specified segment. Furthermore, this approach facilitates an alternative analysis of the relationship between ideal groups and local Galois' torsion groups, encompassing a generalization of local class field theory. In addition, we identify and research distinctocycles associated with the ring R_{1,p} and Kummer theories over valuated local fields. This involves examining the relationship between ideal groups from R_{1,p} and the derived groups of local Galois' torsion groups. In the process, we establish the equivalence between two defined ideals groups from K, thereby extending the scope of local class field theory to include cases with non-trivial modules S. This extension comes with significant implications, especially for fields with characteristic two. We also investigate the connection between our approach and Brueckner-Vostokov's reciprocity law in the characteristic two case. This involves utilizing our local class field theory to derive the required modularity of certain elliptic curves over rational numbers, thereby supporting the specified part of Serre's conjecture. This part specifically deals with cases involving quadratic residues, including those in the ring R_{1,p} and within fields of characteristic two. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
This research paves the way for developing and evaluating other kinds of self-sensing materials to improve the safety of critical engineering projects. 
Furthermore, the proposed framework has the potential to improve the design of these materials by providing precise information about the relationship between electric properties and geometric features that define damage. 
To this end, a nonlinear relationship between scatterers and conductivity changes was investigated to determine how features of conductive inclusions influence the detectability of damage, demonstrating the necessity of optimizing the geometry of nanofillers to achieve maximal conductivity changes in order to enhance the efficacy of the method. 
Finally, the integration of a realistic composite plate model with multiple delaminations and realistic boundary conditions into the reconstruction process is presented, along with the research's limitations and promising areas for future work. 
These areas include evaluating the proposed method on impact-induced damage and delaminations of curved laminates, as well as investigating the effect of fiber orientation on the piezoresistive properties of fiber-reinforced composites.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. In this research, a 128-channel ECoG grid was used to gather data from the motor cortices of healthy subjects but it is anticipated that similar results can be obtained using a higher density grid or even invasive EEG in individuals with spinal cord injuries. This discovery paves the way for the development of a more precise, long-lasting, and clinically applicable BCI for probing and modulating the walking-related neural processes in such patients. This breakthrough also presents an exciting opportunity for the safe control of modern, high-functional lower limb prosthetic devices in individuals with spinal cord injuries. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks on complex data structures. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph connectivity holds significant potential, particularly for tasks like node influence prediction and spread diffusion, but poses a significant challenge due to the high dimensionality of feature inputs. In an effort to bridge this gap, our proposed model, Temporal Graph Attention Network (TGAN), effectively leverages attention mechanisms to dynamically build representations of graph connectivity based on current data and historical information. TGAN achieves a low-dimensional representation of evolving graph connectivity, effectively capturing localized features and neglecting irrelevant information. We support our approach with comprehensive experimental results, demonstrating the superior performance of TGAN in predicting node influence and measuring the spread of information in highly dynamic systems over a range of real-world data sets. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhongyuyu/TGAN.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Events with mid-range initial geometry conditions are found to exhibit radial flow characteristics similar to those in proton-nucleus collisions.  Ultimately, our findings suggest that initial state conditions were influenced by the properties of the medium encountered by the outgoing particles.  Also implied is that the event shape's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient remains unaffected by collision centrality.  Our data are capable of distinguishing between current theoretical models and predicts distinct outcomes when comparing the radial to transverse momentum relations in proton-nucleus and nuclear-nuclear collisions.  Our results are interpretable as indicating substantial radial flow occurrence in the majority of our studied collisions, likely originating from mid-rapidity locations within the collision system.  Our data are further capable of being used to investigate the properties of the medium encountered by outgoing particles, and may also be used to investigate the relationship between radial and elliptic flow phenomena, and even allow for distinction between current theoretical models.  Our results are capable of being used within current theoretical frameworks with the aim of improving the understanding of the physics governing the formation of ultra-relativistic heavy ion systems.  Our data also reveal outcomes that may be difficult to explain using current theoretical models, and as such present a challenge to the scientific community.  Our study covers six different types of event shape variables, and includes data for over 13 million charged particle selections across a range of collision centralities.  Our results for charged hadron distributions exhibit curvature when considering wide transverse momentum ranges, and exhibit little to no dependence on event shape variable type.  Our study's largest findings are presented in a form suitable for use in theoretical model comparisons, and our smaller-scale findings are presented in a form suitable for use in model independence analyses.  Our data are accurate enough to distinguish between current theoretical models, and our study provides the largest and most comprehensive set of data attributes to date in the event shape engineering category.  Our study's methods are a natural extension of existing methods, and our results are capable of being compared directly to existing data

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our code can be downloaded from the website https://github.com/ChenwuChina/DDS. Our findings highlight the significance of accurately modeling particle collisions in simulations of natural flows. Our algorithm has been designed to be adaptable for various types of particles and flows. Our future plans involve refining our algorithm to incorporate the effects of particle collisions on flow turbulence by using LES or DNS schemes. Our goal is to release the code for our research after it is further developed. Our research was supported by the National Science Foundation of China (U19061065, 41929101, 42075103) and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities (2652019012). Our code was developed using OpenFOAM version 7.2 with modifications. Our research was conducted at the Key Laboratory of Water Simulation and Management, Ministry of Education, China. Our simulation results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps lead to excessive deformation of particles, particularly sand grains, due to inadequate resolution of collisions, resulting in inadequate simulation of particle entrainment and turbulence, whereas our algorithm enables accurate simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, preserving the integrity of particles even after extensive collisions. Our algorithm successfully reduced computational cost while maintaining nearly identical accuracy with traditional models, to our knowledge for the first time. Our code is publicly available for downloading from https://github.com/ChenwuChina/DDS. Our research demonstrated that our algorithm effectively mitigates the limitations of traditional models by precisely controlling collision time steps, our code can be used for various applications such as simulation of natural flows with numerous particles

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Additionally, the developed model and controller were validated on a physical robot hopping on a bed of rice grains. The resulting model exhibited accurate predictions of ground reaction forces with respect to displacement, as well as notable robustness when confronted with varying grain sizes and amounts. The research presented here contributes a reliable simulation tool and an empirical model of ground reaction forces suitable for controlling robots on granular terrain. Moreover, the developed controller architecture was found to be effective in commanding specific movements while accommodating the unpredictable nature of ground reaction forces. The findings of this study are relevant to the control of robots navigating other deformable terrains, including those with complex geometric structures and multiple degrees of freedom. The effect of feedback control on the developed model was examined in relation to its stability and robustness. The research presented here provides a useful framework for the control of robots moving on soft ground with the aim of precisely executing movement tasks while accounting for the uncertainty associated with ground deformation. The developed approach was found to be applicable to various types of soft terrain, thereby contributing meaningfully to the knowledge in this field. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving accurate hierarchies, as measured by a range of metrics, including the coherence of sub-tree topics and the accuracy of document classifications. Furthermore, our model exhibits the ability to automatically detect hierarchical levels and accurately classify individual documents within the network. We have made our code and associated models publicly available to facilitate further research in this area. Empirical evaluations conducted on HDTM suggest that it performs significantly better than the current state-of-the-art methods, achieving an average 5% increase in classification accuracy across all datasets tested. We have also released our code and models publicly to support ongoing and future research on HDTM. 

To demonstrate the applicability of HDTM in real-world applications, we created a prototype search engine that leverages our model and incorporates features such as personalized hierarchies based on user feedback, see our accompanying video at this link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2nJ3D9sLaGw. This video shows a user interacting with our search engine and provides an illustration of how hierarchies can be adapted to suit individual needs. We have made the code and models associated with this search engine prototype publicly available as well, to facilitate ongoing research in this domain. 

Finally, we acknowledge the limitations of our current model, particularly its reliance on supervised learning for document classification, and highlight potential avenues for future research, such as developing unsupervised strategies for evaluating the quality of generated hierarchies. We also outline the challenges involved in integrating multiple information networks and provide an example of how to combine Wikipedia content with additional knowledge bases, see our accompanying notebook at this link: https://github.com/alexbardo/HierarchicalDocumentTopicModel/blob/main/notebooks/10_Merging_Networks.ipynb. This notebook demonstrates the steps needed to conduct such an integration and offers guidelines for future work in this area

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately identify the annealing gap, as demonstrated through simulations of quantum spin models and their application to a genetic optimization problem. Furthermore, we show that the quench parameter retains its relevance even in scenarios featuring multiple annealing gap minima, making it a reliable indicator of the optimal quench parameter, thereby providing a straightforward and general method for finding the quench parameter that yields the smallest annealing gap. This discovery is particularly significant given the growing interest in quantum annealing and its variants, as it offers a straightforward and universally applicable method for determining the optimal quench parameter, which is increasingly crucial in addressing complex optimization challenges. This research paves the way for further exploration of the interconnection between quench and annealing dynamics, as well as the potential utility of the quench parameter as an indicator of performance in various quantum annealing scenarios. This study employs the dynamical quench parameter to reckon the annealing gap, which is crucial to improving approximate quantum annealing algorithms, as demonstrated through the simulation of the quantum adiabatic algorithm on various spin Hamiltonians, including the Heisenberg model, Dimer model, and Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model. Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band

which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, this study underlines the potential pitfalls of over-simplifying
complex band structures and highlights the need for careful consideration of
screening in layered nickelates.

As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be used in compact star research.  This new type of quark star equation of states exhibits increased sound velocity in dense matter, which could, in turn, influence the dynamics of compact stars as detected via gravitational waves. Our work paves the way for investigating the hadron-quark phase transition's properties from sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron and hybrid stars. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters. Additionally, both states exhibit analogous variance characteristics when coherent amplitude is large, offering potential utility in estimating intense drive amplitudes. Despite sharing many properties with the compass state, the proposed ensemble is more robust against high average photon number, making it a viable option for sensitive parameter estimation in such scenarios.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Our analysis accounted for various astronomical phenomena, including the movements of stars, the refraction of light through the medium surrounding a satellite, and the satellite's movement. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Moreover, an in-depth error analysis is conducted to identify knowledge acquisition errors and guide future improvements. The knowledge-aware approach is also applied to a coarse-to-fine search strategy, resulting in enhanced performance on the MuTual Sensemaking dataset. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. It is essential to note that a comprehensive analysis of all possible cations present in a comet is not feasible, as many variables influence the composition of cometary neutral gas, making comprehensive spectrum analysis crucial for accurate comprehension. Suggested observational priorities aim to enhance the comprehension of the cometary neutral gas composition at specific altitudes within a comet and could be met using existing space-based spectrographs on board the Rosetta mission's Orbital Wide Angle Camera or the Cosmic Wide Band instrument on the Solar and Heliosophysical Laboratory's spacecraft. It is also necessary to conduct laboratory studies of cationic molecules at temperatures mimicking those found in cometary atmospheres, which could be achieved using a newly developed infrared-UV photoelectric dissociation apparatus. Ultimately, enhancing the reference spectral data will facilitate a more accurate analysis of cometary spectra, refining the comprehension of the local plasma environments and allowing the search for volatile compounds in cometary neutral gas. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. To validate our approach, an optimized gradient descent method is implemented and testing results are provided on both synthetic and real-world datasets showing the efficacy of our method. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A broader analysis considering the value of lives saved as a result of reduced homicide rates and the decrease in future injury crimes suggests that the economic benefits of providing treatment likely far exceed the associated costs.  Consequently, denying court-ordered mental health treatment as part of a sentence appears to increase the chances of an offender returning to the justice system and violating their probation leading to a higher likelihood of incarceration.  From an economic perspective providing treatment also yields a significant return-on-investment by covering and exceeding associated expenses and in addition presenting substantial external benefits that could be captured through incentive-based policies.  Ultimately this analysis implies that rather than being viewed as an added expense court-ordered mental health treatment as part of a sentence should be seen as a valuable tool that reduces future crime and yields a substantial return-on-investment.  As such justice systems across the globe may benefit from adopting policies that prioritize the delivery of court-ordered mental health treatment to those within the justice system who require it.  To achieve this goal payment for performance schemes could be established that reward justice systems and corrections officers for the successful delivery of court-ordered mental health treatment and thereby provide an added incentive to prioritize the successful rehabilitation of offenders.  This reward could be based on the reduction in future crime rates among those who receive court-ordered mental health treatment and as such would directly tie the performance payment to the delivery of a specific justice outcome of greater community benefit.  This could also help address the current challenge faced by many low- and middle-income countries that struggle to provide effective and efficient justice services due in large part to inadequate incentives facing justice system officials.
