When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. Notably, a notable application of rotationally invariant L1-PCA in magnetic resonance imaging is discussed, involving an interesting regularization technique to obtain a low-rank component. This represents a novel application of L1-PCA and a method of achieving regularization via the same method used for data representation. Empirical results show that this approach yields higher PSNR values compared to the widely used VBMRI technique. A suitable choice of algorithm parameters is crucial for achieving this model's representation, and an additional experiment was conducted to examine the relationship between the algorithm parameters and results of image reconstruction. In this experiment, the relationship between the algorithm parameters and results of image reconstruction were examined, and suitable default parameters were suggested for future users. To ensure the validity of the methodology, the algorithm was additionally tested on synthetic datasets without anomalies to compare its performance with the established sparse PCA and rotationally invariant PCA algorithms. This comparison confirmed that the proposed algorithm performs comparably in terms of reconstruction error, but is superior in terms of the number of components retained when the true components follow a single cluster distribution. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. Furthermore, this approach may be adapted to investigate magnetic field interactions with atomic spins in quantum systems or potentially reveal novel aspects of superconductivity in materials. 

A key component in realizing this proposal involves developing a atomic interferometry setup with sufficient resolution to detect minute changes in atomic motion caused by local magnetic field gradients. This goal is within the technical capabilities of the current generation of atomic physics laboratories. A theoretical analysis of how expelled local magnetic field effects behave in different superconducting material shapes has also been conducted. This includes discussions on how to measure expelled field gradients near the surface of superconductors and analyzing the reach of atomic interferometry in this context. Ultimately, this research paves the way for exploring novel quantum phenomena at the interface between atomic and condensed matter physics. It is also important to note that exploiting atomic interferometry to detect the meissner effect is a concept that was initially proposed by Steve Kassa.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As a concrete example of DynaSOAr's capabilities, we show how to modify the Alberi search algorithm to make it compatible with DynaSOAr, and in turn unlock the algorithm's potential by transforming it into an SMMO application.  As a result, we are able to successfully search for 128 million keys using only 1GB of memory in approximately 1 second on an NVIDIA V100 GPU.  Conversely, the original version of the algorithm is limited to search spans of up to 10 million keys due to memory constraints, making DynaSOAr's extension an appealing solution for various real-world applications.  Ultimately, DynaSOAr's user-friendly nature is showcased by the addition of a simple string search example that can be easily replicated by any developer.  In addition to DynaSOAr, we also publicly release the Alberi search algorithm as another useful contribution.  Lastly, we highlight the broad applicability of the SMMO paradigm on high-performance computing devices, coupled with the advent of unified memory architecture, as opportunities for future research and development.  To facilitate this, we outline a potential new research direction for massively parallel object-oriented memory management on modern computing

In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data and combining it with spectroscopic analysis from $TESS$, $Kepler$, and $SPITZER$, astronomers determined that TOI-712 is approximately 500 million years old and contains planets with sizes ranging from Earth to Jupiter. The researchers believe that TOI-712's planetary system underwent significant evolution over its first billion years due to external influences such as tidal interactions with a nearby massive planet or migration induced by its own protoplanetary disk. This phenomenon could be more widespread than initially thought and highlights the importance of considering factors like tidal interactions, migration, and external influences on the development of young planets. This study also highlights the importance of $TESS$ discoveries in allowing the study of rare and complex planetary systems that would be harder to find with other telescopes. Furthermore, TOI-712's age provides an ideal opportunity to examine the planet's surface composition using spectroscopic analysis from $TESS$ and $SPITZER$, which revealed that the two larger planets have atmospheres, with one being highly inflated and the other having a possible rocky surface. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties. We also evaluated the barrier to this water decomposition reaction and found that TiO2 with appropriate doping possesses a lowered barrier of only 1.45 eV as opposed to 2.73 eV for undoped material. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. For the standard model, the limit on the effective electromagnetic coupling of the top quark is $\kappa_t < 0.13$, surpassing the effective coupling measurable through top-quark pair production in the leptonic channel. This detection method also opens the door for constraining certain beyond the Standard Model theories, leading to a lower bound on the mass of a new scalar particle contributing to the effective electromagnetic coupling of the top quark at $\mathcal{O}(300)$ GeV. This research was motivated by the effective Lagrangian approach to describing the effective electromagnetic coupling of the top quark, specifically the Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}_{eff} = \kappa_t \frac{\alpha G_F}{\sqrt{2}} (\bar{u} \gamma_\mu u + \bar{c} \gamma_\mu c) W^\mu_\nu \bar{t} D^\nu t + h.c.$. For this effective Lagrangian, the limit on $\kappa_t$ scales with the energy of the proton-proton collisions. For the 13 TeV collision energy of the LHC, the limit on $\kappa_t$ is $\kappa_t < 0.017$, which is insensitive to the integrated luminosity of the dataset. This research was further explored in a companion paper discussing the simulation requirements and detailing the theoretical foundations of the effective Lagrangian approach. This detection method is made possible by the CMS TOTEM luminosity measurement system operating during the 2015 run of the LHC. This research was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and the National Science Foundation. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Dr. Yves Sirois. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, under certain conditions. It is essential to note that the degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted electrons as well as the density of the target pre-fill. Furthermore, it is possible to increase the produced charge to several hundred nanocoulombs by optimizing the target pre-fill, at the cost of lower polarization levels. Our data are supported by theoretical explanations based on the analysis of emitted electrons and positrons in the context of their own electromagnetic fields. It is worth mentioning that the achievement of such high densities of polarized positrons through other means is extremely challenging with current technology. Therefore, interacting intense lasers with solid targets may provide a viable method for producing polarized positrons at unprecedented scales. It is also necessary to note that the property of polarized positrons decay rapidly over time as they interact with the emitted photons within the plasma, making the direct observation of such phenomena challenging. Nevertheless, this phenomenon offers a novel method of studying the decay of intense electric fields in the context of particle physics. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. This work also provides an infinite family of groups with a constant diameter and infinite nilpotency class as well as two distinct finite group families with variable polynomial diameter and infinite nilpotency class. This work builds upon earlier results from Breuillard and Tointon. This research was conducted while holding a Postdoctoral Fellowship from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Council of Canada. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes an effortless voltage regulation capability, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage changes. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was integrated into a 65nm test chip employing adaptive voltage and frequency scaling, demonstrating the versatility of the design. Given its outstanding performance, the proposed temperature sensor is suitable for a wide range of applications, from embedded systems to Internet of Things devices. The design is available through the Open-Hardware collaboration platform, allowing researchers to leverage the temperature sensor's capabilities for various purposes. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  It is also crucial to investigate the sufficient conditions for a core to break down and give birth to a massive star or a low-mass star.  We propose that a necessary condition for massive star formation could be the presence of massive cores with particular density characteristics, in particular, densities exceeding 7 x 10^4 g/cm^3, and we suggest carrying out large molecular weight element abundance mappings at the cores' centers to verify this hypothesis.  This research adds to the existing understanding of massive star formation with massive, optically bright protostars as the end products, and it also contributes to the existing knowledge about the formation of massive, optically invisible protostars.  This discovery may be applied to other infrared dark clouds, which are known to house massive star formation activity, and it could be a crucial element in developing their core evolution models.  Finally, it is also crucial to explore the necessary conditions for a core to break down and give birth to a massive star or a low-mass star, and the necessary steps for this to happen are not yet entirely understood.  This work paves the way for large-scale molecular weight element abundance mappings at the cores' centers, which are necessary to verify the proposed necessary condition for massive star formation, namely the presence of very dense cores.  This research opens up new avenues for investigating the formation of massive star formation with massive, optically bright protostars as the end products as well as the formation of massive, optically invisible protostars.  This work also contributes to the existing knowledge about the formation of massive star formation within infrared dark clouds, which are known to house such activity.  This discovery can be applied to other infrared dark clouds and is a crucial element in developing their core evolution models.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. These operators are analogous to the conventional differentiation and integration operators used for polynomial families, such as Jacobi and Laguerre polynomials. The construction of these operators is achieved through the use of weighted sums of the conventional operators, taking into account the distinct characteristics of Gegenbauer polynomials, ensuring that the (strict) positive definiteness is maintained. The resulting operators are explicitly defined and demonstrated to satisfy the desired properties, including the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness and the increase of the space dimension by one. The paper also delves into the composition of these operators and provides examples of their application in specific contexts. The constructed operators have the potential to be useful in the construction of positive definite functions on spaces of higher dimensions, particularly those based on the sphere, and may be employed in various numerical methods, such as the Nystrom method. The paper also outlines the relationship between these operators and the conventional methods of differentiation and integration, as well as their connection to the Gegenbauer transform and the use of weighted sums. The last section of the paper presents numerical results obtained using the Nystrom method with the constructed operators, demonstrating their effectiveness and accuracy in achieving positive definite functions of higher dimensions. The paper also provides the code used for these numerical experiments. The code is written in the MATLAB programming language and is publicly available online. The numerical experiments were conducted using a Linux operating system with the GCC compiler, and the results were obtained using the CRAY XC30 and IBM NeXtScale Double, high-performance computers. The paper also outlines the requirements for running the code, which includes the MATLAB programming language and the GECO toolbox. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. This factor determines whether surface contacts or border connections primarily resist motion. The study provides evidence of surface contacts generating additional resistance during stick-slip motion and offers insights for modeling other non-Newtonian fluids flowing over rough surfaces. The approach we used can be applied to other interfacial flows with similar dynamics. The stick-slip regime is temperature-dependent and transforms to the surface slippage regime with increasing temperature. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. The code and guidelines for the winning project have been made publicly available.

Additionally, an analysis of attention maps reveals the presence of the proposed look-ahead attention effect in many cases, despite the small size of our translated chains. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Furthermore, we outline the challenges faced by grid computing and highlight potential opportunities for future development. Additionally, we provide mature projects such as Apache Airflow and Slurm as suitable examples of translational computer science projects. Finally, we highlight potential opportunities for grid computing in the face of rising computational demands and declining funding support. Despite facing significant challenges, grid computing remains a viable option for processing massive computational tasks. We conclude by emphasizing the significance of grid computing in the scientific community and encouraging researchers to contribute to its development. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, researchers investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. The results indicate that the model exhibits a triple-point structure, which corresponds to the transition from an adiabatic to a bulk viscous phase, and finally to a dust-like phase. This results in a non-linear behaviour for the system's variables in time, and the features of this non-linearity are analysed in depth. Moreover, the model shows both periodic and chaotic behaviours in the phase space, which are both triggered by the same parameter that drives the transition to non-linearity, but are determined by different initial conditions. The model's dynamics are also compared to observational data for the Hubble parameter, which indicates that the model is capable of explaining the local Hubble anomaly, but the behaviour of the Hubble parameter in the model relies on a constant viscosity coefficient, which makes it difficult to distinguish the model from other dark energy models. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Furthermore, this approach resolves another common issue with U-Net based models, where masks are often over-smoothed. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, it was applied to a dataset consisting of liver biopsy images, with notable improvements in performance benchmarks. Additionally, this approach was found to yield comparable performance when compared to state-of-the-art models using U-Net architecture, following model fine-tuning. To demonstrate its practical value, it was also used to extract valuable information from previously detected nuclei, with encouraging results. In summary, this research presents a distinctive solution to the complications involved in pathology image analysis, and showcases the feasibility of using a W-shaped network to extract valuable information from pre-labeled nuclei. Moreover, it highlights the potential applications of this approach in scenarios where prior knowledge is available. With the additional code provided online, this research aims to contribute to the advancement of pathology image analysis technology. To ensure scalability, the approach proposed in this research is designed such that the W-shaped network architecture can be used as a baseline for other, more complex architectures. To facilitate reproducibility, the code provided online includes not only the W-shaped network code, but also the data preprocessing scripts used in the liver biopsy image analysis experiments presented in this research. Furthermore, it includes the evaluation metrics calculation scripts.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of the partial converse theorem for the automorphic representation of GL(N) with a gamma factor established by Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai. Furthermore, our result extends the works by Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai as well as by Jiang and Soudry on the partial converse theorems for the GL(N) and the classical group cases respectively. It is worth noting that our result also encompasses the results on the supercyclicity part due to the specific nature of the gamma factors involved. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of semi-simple groups with gamma factors, for which we establish the local converse theorem, and subsequently apply this insight to solve our representation isomorphism problem. This approach relies on an inductive argument that we can reduce the problem of determining the isomorphism of two given representations to a related problem of representation isomorphism for a lower-dimensional group with shared gamma factors, for which we can then apply our earlier result on the supercyclicity of irreducible automorphic representations. This representation isomorphism for the lower-dimensional group is then achieved through an inductive process on the dimension of the group. This inductive process itself is realized by an iterative process on the Bessel transforms of the irreducible automorphic representations of the lower-dimensional group, for which we can establish the necessary properties, including the property of shared gamma factors, necessary to apply our earlier result on the supercyclicity of these representations. This approach enables us to overcome various obstacles posed by the lack of known results on the converse theorem for the Bessel transforms of the irreducible automorphic representations of the lower-dimensional group. This result on the representation isomorphism for G also encompasses the results on the converse theorem for the twisted and the untwisted cases of the symplectic

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Ultimately, this comprehensive study on GCNNs yields valuable insights into their automatic feature extraction capability and reinforces the notion that GCNNs represent a unified, overarching framework encompassing diverse Neural Network architectures. We further examine the relationship between GCNN parameters and those of traditional CNNs, facilitating a straightforward pathway to interpreting GCNN learning processes and their underlying mechanics. To enhance reader engagement, this technical exploration is supported by an accompanying interactive web-based learning tool that allows for an engaging, hands-on experience with GCNN learning processes. This study and the accompanying educational platform are both valuable resources for both seasoned professionals and students looking to understand the inner workings of GCNNs. We anticipate that this research will also contribute to the development of educational materials and learning tools focused on GCNNs. We have made our findings and the accompanying educational platform available on the GCNN Learning website at www.gcnlearn.com. We look forward to feedback from the community. We have also included the code for the web-based learning tool on the GCNN Learning website at www.gcnlearn.com/code, in addition to contributing it to the wider research community. We believe that the unique, interactive nature of this web-based learning tool sets it apart from other educational resources focused on GCNNs. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Consequently, VSSA- OVERWIND elastography exhibits superior performance in estimating tissue mechanical properties, particularly in the assessment of liver tissues. The technique's advantages come with minimal investment in hardware, making it an attractive option for the medical community. The proposed method demonstrates notable advancements in elastography, showcasing its potential for expanding deep tissue imaging capabilities. The technique's major drawback lies in its reliance on high-performance ultrasound processing devices. The VSSA- OVERWIND technique presents a promising future for elastography, particularly in the assessment of soft liver tissues, albeit with the need for further development to accommodate diverse ultrasound processing configurations. The research provides valuable insights into the optimization of beamforming algorithms for elastography, emphasizing the need for balanced settings that strike a harmony between lateral resolution, sampling frequency, and signal-to-noise ratio. The outcome highlights the importance of processing ultrasound data with consideration for the elastography application at hand. The study's outcomes are available for use by the medical community, having been made open-source by the authors. Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining dimension-independent output. We achieve this by introducing a new metric called coordinate span ratio and utilizing it to monitor specific coordinate values across the dataset. These values are adjusted in response to added or removed data points, enabling us to maintain a representative set of coordinates. Furthermore, we demonstrate the accuracy of our solution by examining its error relative to an ideal solution under various conditions. As an additional contribution, we establish a lower bound on the required storage capacity for a general class of coreset algorithms utilized to solve streaming $k$-means clustering problems. This lower bound provides insight into the design of future coreset algorithms and confirms the optimality of our solution for high-dimensional datasets. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Furthermore, our approach facilitates meaningful policy interpretations by highlighting the importance of specific states in the game. Our method's effectiveness is highlighted in a series of simulations testing its performance in various settings. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. To our knowledge, this study is the first to explore the application
of learned dynamics models in multi-task reinforcement learning settings. Our
results provide insights into the behavior of learned dynamics models and reveal
effective ways to extend their capabilities to multiple tasks. Our approach can
be viewed as a form of dynamic task embedding, where the model represents each
task as a distinct intrinsic state of the learned environment. Our work also
opens up significant research questions in areas like transfer learning dynamics
models and neural network decomposition. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/hoangduy1992/multitaskMBRL. Our results can be utilized as benchmarks for the community in the field of reinforcement learning. Our approach has the benefit of being generally applicable to any set of related tasks and can be viewed as a way to dynamically embed tasks within the learned environment. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Another screen, at a distance of 6.05 parsecs, exhibits distinct characteristics and may be linked to a nearby molecular cloud. Both screens were found to be stationary over the observed time period, whereas three other screens were detected at greater distances (between 7.5 and 9.5 parsecs) and exhibited relative movements towards the Sun, likely as a result of their position within the local interstellar medium flows. These results provide the first detailed investigation of screens in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 and contribute to the understanding of the local interstellar medium structures observed in the surrounding area up to a distance of 10 parsecs from the Sun. The methods employed in this research can be applied to the study of other pulsars and their associated screens in the interstellar medium. The data used in this analysis are available upon request from the Arecibo Observatory Pulsar Database. The related parameters for the screens detected around PSR B1133+16 are presented in the accompanying tables and figures. The research described in this paper was funded by NSF grant AST-1414752. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, a Quasi-Periodic WaveNet-based text-to-speech system is constructed and proven to be highly effective in controlling the pitch for non-standard speaker identities and ages. This is achieved by employing a cascaded network with a small size, focused on speech prosody, in conjunction with a large, universally applicable QuPNet as the base generator network. This yields an significant improvement in the fundamental frequency accuracy and naturalness of the synthesized speech in comparison to conventional approaches. This research's findings are validated through extensive experiments and potentially offer technological advancements for the generation of quasi-periodic signals in various speech and non-speech domains. This research's QuPNet model is also made publicly available for future studies. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, the analysis into shadows facilitates a more in-depth examination of the structure of THH, thereby shedding light on the more general characteristics of the functors defined on it. The study also delves into the characteristics of THH in the context of enriched categories, encompassing both graded categories and filtered categories. The resulting shadow envelopes are found to exhibit Morita invariance, thereby yielding distinct and distinguishing bicategorical interpretations of the original category. The analysis presented in this research is applicable to a broad spectrum of categories, including those with modules over rings, algebras, and Hopf algebras, among others. The ultimate conclusion drawn from this exploration is that the functors defined on THH can be essentially viewed as intrinsic properties of the original bicategory, thereby endowing a heightened status of universality upon the associated shadow envelope. The research on shadow envelopes is also used as a key tool in the analysis of the properties of THH in relation to the structure of the original category, thereby uncovering new characteristics and differences. The study presented here is comprised of introductory elements, more comprehensive and detailed versions of which are presented in the accompanying appendices. The primary purpose of these appendices is to provide a standalone understanding of the theory of shadow envelopes. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our source code and VGG-Sound Source dataset are available for public use at this link: https://github.com/yangzw123/vggsound_source.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have explored GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN is a straightforward extension to homogeneous models, and it is numerically shown to be more effective than other geometric GCNs in Euclidean space. This is particularly evident when applying it to linear structures, e.g., Ziegler's theorem on linear graphs. For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, the Weyl-Wigner symbolic formulation yields a straightforward expression of the thermal equilibrium state's density operator. This expression is characterized by a single matrix variable, enabling an intuitive derivation of the equilibrium state's thermodynamic properties. In contrast, more general Hamiltonians require more complex Weyl-Wigner representations, making it less straightforward to determine the equilibrium state's properties. However, this paper demonstrates that for any Hamiltonian, the equilibrium state can be expressed in terms of a single Weyl-Wigner variable, specifically in a phase-space representation based on the symplectic vector. A key aspect of this representation is that it results in a $2 \times 2$ matrix, whose trace yields the equilibrium state's density. A range of thermodynamic quantities, including temperature-dependent correlations and the equilibrium state's density, can be determined directly from this representation. Ultimately, this paper shows that the equilibrium state's properties rely solely on this $2 \times 2$ matrix, enabling a comprehensive understanding of its behavior. A notable corollary of this finding is that the equilibrium state's behavior is essentially two-dimensional, exhibiting all the essential features observed in one-dimensional quantum systems. A central aspect of this paper's results is validated through the application of our approach to a specific model, namely, a discrete, one-dimensional XY chain. Notably, our analysis of this chain reveals that its equilibrium state's behavior can be accurately described using a two-dimensional matrix, specifically the XY chain's lattice counterpart of the Ginzburg-Landau equation's coefficient matrix. This finding provides a new perspective on the XY chain's equilibrium state's behavior, showcasing its two-dimensional character. A key aspect of this paper's results is also its relevance to continuous, one-dimensional XY chains, demonstrating that the corresponding equilibrium state's behavior can be accurately described using a two-dimensional matrix, namely the Ginzburg-Landau equation's coefficient matrix. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we highlight the implications of this concept for quantum systems and provide an example involving photons in a cavity based on earlier research findings. These findings, published in Physical Review A, demonstrated that negative absolute temperature can be achieved and maintained within quantum systems, fulfilling the prerequisite conditions necessary for true negative temperatures. A crucial point to emphasize is that we distinguish true negative temperatures from the apparent illusion of them, which can arise in systems exhibiting energy degeneracy. A key aspect of our discussion involves the relationship between these apparent fake negative temperatures and true negative temperatures, including the condition of energy degeneracy necessary for the occurrence of the latter. We also explore the possibility of obtaining negative absolute temperatures within both quantum and classical harmonic oscillators, demonstrating the distinction between true and fake negative temperatures. Notably, we highlight the potential applications of true negative temperatures in quantum systems, such as photons in a cavity, and the resulting non-degenerate quantum thermodynamics, which we believe holds significant promise for future research. A comprehensive bibliography is provided at the end of this report. It is worth noting that the initial idea for this report originated from a lecture delivered at the 12th International Summer School on Quantum Physics, held in Varna, Bulgaria in 2019. The associated lecture notes are also included in the bibliography. The concept of negative absolute temperature is not new and was first proposed theoretically in the 1950s. However, the first experimental confirmation of negative absolute temperature was achieved in 2011 among atoms rather than photons. It is worth noting that the term negative absolute temperature is sometimes referred to as "frozen" or "negative temperature". It is also worth mentioning that the idea of temperature below absolute zero is often associated with the work of Sir James Jeans, who first proposed it in the 1920s. The mathematics of negative absolute temperature were first introduced in the context of two-level systems and then expanded to include quantum and classical harmonic oscillators. The associated physics and mathematics are often misunderstood, particularly with regards to the distinction between true and apparent negative temperatures. The condition necessary for true negative temperatures, namely energy degeneracy, is not always met in laboratory settings.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. By integrating the renormalization group equations up to two-loop order, we calculate the self-energy corrections to the Higgs mass, arriving at the conclusion that the Higgs mass falls within the 125 GeV standard model experiment's allowed range. Moreover, we identify the minimal scenario in which the top quark Yukawa coupling remains within the perturbative regime up to the grand unification scale. We also examine the predictions for low-energy phenomena, including neutrinoless double beta decay, lepton-flavor violation in rare decays, and rare Higgs decay patterns. We analyze multiple variant scenarios to demonstrate the ease with which the simplest scoto-seesaw model accommodates the observed Higgs mass and dark matter properties. We explore various extensions of the simplest scoto-seesaw model, examining the impact of additional fermions in the dark sector on the neutrino oscillation lengths and other low-energy phenomena. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The software is designed for paragliding
competition analysis but can be utilized for data examination across various
fields. ViDaExpert is available for Windows operating systems. Despite being
user-friendly, the application also offers an API for scripting and
programmatic use. The API is accessible via Python through the pyvida package.
